documents.abstract: The global financial ecosystem is undergoing a profound transformation with the integration of advanced digital technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI). Financial markets that once relied heavily on human intuition and traditional analytical methods are increasingly adopting AI-driven tools to enhance investment decision-making, risk assessment, and portfolio management. The rise of AI has significantly reshaped how investors interact with financial information, enabling more data-driven, efficient, and predictive investment strategies. At the same time, the financial system itself has evolved into two major structures: centralized finance (CeFi) and decentralized finance (DeFi). Technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, and predictive analytics allow financial institutions to analyze large volumes of financial data and generate investment insights with high accuracy. The convergence of AI with these two financial systems is creating new opportunities and challenges for investors

Artificial intelligence is reshaping entrepreneurial financial management, yet its relationship with business performance in emerging economies remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities view and the technology–organization–environment perspective, this study examines how intelligent financial analytics and automated FinTech services relate to entrepreneurial performance through financial agility, with AI readiness as a moderator. Online survey data from business owners, founders, and entrepreneurs in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, Pakistan, were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Both intelligent financial analytics and automated FinTech services were positively associated with financial agility and entrepreneurial performance. Financial agility partially mediated these relationships, while AI readiness strengthened the associations between both technologies and agility, as well as between agility and performance. Conditional indirect effects were greater at higher levels of readiness. These findings identify financial agility as a potential mechanism connecting financial technologies with entrepreneurial outcomes and highlight readiness as a boundary condition. The study suggests that entrepreneurs and policymakers should complement technology adoption with investments in digital infrastructure, data quality, employee skills, and leadership support for effective implementation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming fashion e-commerce through personalized recommendations, virtual try-on, size suggestions, and algorithmic decision support. This study examines AI-driven fit confidence as a fashion-specific mechanism linking AI personalization quality, algorithmic transparency, trust in AI, consumer experience, and purchase intention, while considering privacy concern as a boundary condition. Data from 400 Ecuadorian consumers with prior exposure to AI-enabled recommendation or personalization features in fashion e-commerce were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. AI personalization quality and trust in AI were positively associated with fit confidence, while algorithmic transparency was associated with trust in AI. Fit confidence was strongly related to consumer experience but showed only a small direct association with purchase intention; its indirect effect through consumer experience was substantially larger, indicating complementary partial mediation. Privacy concern had no significant direct relationship with fit confidence. The interaction between privacy concern and personalization quality was negative, but evidence was mixed and sensitive to the bootstrap confidence-interval method; H7 was not supported under the primary percentile-bootstrap criterion adopted in this study. Predictive analyses showed stronger out-of-sample performance for trust in AI and fit confidence than for purchase intention. The study distinguishes trust in technology from confidence in anticipated product–consumer fit and supports explainable, privacy-sensitive applications in fashion e-commerce.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming information retrieval through natural language processing, machine learning, semantic search, and intelligent interfaces. These developments offer opportunities to improve information access for persons with physical disabilities but may also create exclusion when systems fail to address users’ physical, technological, and behavioral needs This review examines literature published between 2016 and 2026 on AI-driven information retrieval, accessibility, information-seeking behavior, and information use among individuals with physical disabilities, with particular attention to Nigerian evidence. Findings indicate that persons with physical disabilities have significant educational, health, social, recreational, and personal information needs and increasingly rely on online and electronic information. Studies identify persistent barriers, including inadequate resources, inaccessible facilities, limited assistive technologies, difficulty locating information, and insufficient accommodation for them in most libraries. AI adoption in Nigerian libraries remains constrained by infrastructure, funding, skills, connectivity, ethical concerns, and institutional readiness. International evidence shows that AI can improve accessibility through adaptive interfaces, personalised retrieval, speech interaction, recommendations, and assistive technologies. However, research focuses more on visual disabilities than physical impairments. Major concerns include algorithmic bias, inaccessible interfaces, privacy and limited user participation. The review recommends collaborative user involvement in design, accessibility-focused development, and compatibility with assistive technologies, flexible search interfaces, and user-centered assessment.

BACKGROUND Artificial intelligence (AI)–driven lifestyle interventions are increasingly used for reducing diabetes risk. However, whether they produce clinical benefit beyond standard Diabetes Prevention Programs (DPPs) and whether effects vary by AI type, population, or delivery setting, remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to evaluate the effects of AI-driven lifestyle interventions on clinical, behavioral, and engagement outcomes among people with prediabetes or elevated diabetes risk and to assess whether effects differed by AI type, population, or delivery setting. METHODS PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ClinicalTrials.gov, and citation searches were completed on August 3, 2026, for English-language reports published from 2015. Eligible studies evaluated AI-driven digital lifestyle interventions among people with prediabetes or elevated diabetes risks, or healthy participants in feasibility studies. One reviewer (OIE) screened records and extracted data; a second reviewer (TN) independently verified exclusions and extraction. Study quality was assessed with National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute tools appropriate to each design. Given substantial heterogeneity in designs, estimands, and outcome metrics, findings were synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis guideline rather than pooled statistically. RESULTS Of 8032 records, 11 studies were included: 1 randomized, 1 nonrandomized comparative, 4 observational, and 5 uncontrolled pre-post studies. Seven evaluated AI lifestyle coaching systems, 2 predictive AI platforms, and 2 conversational AI chatbots. Ten of 11 studies used commercially developed platforms. Study quality was rated good for 5 studies, fair for 3, and poor for 3. The randomized controlled trial showed noninferiority of an AI-DPP versus human coach–led DPP for the combined 12-month outcome (23/183, 12.6% vs 23/185, 12.4%; risk difference 0.1%, 1-sided 95% CI –5.5%). Program initiation (171/183, 93.4% vs 153/185, 82.7%; risk difference 10.7%, 95% CI 4.2%-17.3%) and completion (117/183, 63.9% vs 93/185, 50.3%; risk difference 13.7%; 95% CI 3.6%-23.7%) were higher with AI, but this did not translate into superior clinical outcomes. The nonrandomized comparison found no advantage of AI-personalized messaging over static messaging in terms of BMI or physical activity. The remaining studies reported uncontrolled changes precluding causal inference. Evidence was insufficient to determine whether effects differed by population or delivery setting. CONCLUSIONS One randomized trial supports noninferiority, not superiority, of a specific AI-driven DPP relative to human coaching; the remaining evidence was nonrandomized, predominantly commercially developed, and hypothesis-generating. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review to stratify evidence on AI-driven diabetes prevention by AI mechanism—coaching, predictive, and conversational—and by outcome domain, extending prior scoping work that mapped apps without appraising study quality or comparative effectiveness. This structured mapping shows where evidence is the strongest (engagement and weight) and the weakest (glycemic causality and generalizability), giving health systems a concrete basis for deciding where AI-DPP tools may supplement, rather than replace, standard DPP delivery, pending independent, adequately powered randomized trials.

Customer experience (CX) is transformed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create value through AI advancement, with the collaboration of people for personalization and transparent interactions across the digital journey to gain a competitive advantage. This chapter creates premises that integrate and resolve contradictions in research on how CX creates value by using AI. Six literature fields were identified by a systematic review of articles that address how AI enables CX and value in the long term. To establish the research traditions by comparing the key concepts and metatheoretical assumptions addressed by each literature field, two concepts arise from analysis: customer experience and value emerge through AI advancement and adoption without human assistance, or it emerges through Human-AI collaboration. Identifying the alignment using a metatheoretical lens by research traditions forms four premises. These premises help to develop concepts about how experience creates value in the AI-driven world by explaining its framework and developing ideas for the future

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learning technologies have significantly transformed financial markets and replaced intuition based strategies by data-driven intelligent systems. AI-driven trading and portfolio optimization platforms, which integrate advanced analytics, predictive modeling, and automated decision-making to enhance investment performance. The chapter explores the design and application of AI enabled trading platforms in modern financial markets. These platforms support technologies such as machine learning algorithms, deep learning models, natural language processing, and big data analytics to analyze market trends, detect trading opportunities, and construct optimized investment portfolios. By combining real-time and historical data, AI generate predictive insights for informed investment decisions and risk management strategies. The chapter discusses the evolution of algorithmic trading and AI's growing role in financial market analysis. It examines key components including data acquisition modules, predictive analytics engines, automated trading systems, and portfolio optimization models. Challenges such as model interpretability, regulatory compliance, data privacy, and algorithmic bias are also addressed. A conceptual framework is proposed for effective deployment of these technologies.

Generative AI is reshaping higher education's instructional video production, a domain once limited by cost, time, and specialized skills. This review examines how text-to-video synthesis, synthetic voice, automated editing, and AI-assisted authoring fit into the production lifecycle. Drawing on research from 2023–2026, it maps these tools against pre-production, production, and post-production stages, distinguishing between cognitive augmentation and output acceleration. Findings show AI-generated videos match traditional ones in learning outcomes while boosting efficiency, scalability, and multilingual access. However, risks include factual errors, loss of authenticity, and inequitable access. Contextualized within Philippine and ASEAN higher education, the chapter proposes a three-stage adoption framework (policy/governance, capability building, and equitable resourcing) to help educators adopt AI responsibly, concluding with policy implications.

Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled human resource (HR) practices foster agile talent deployment within startup firms, particularly highlighting the mediating role of trust in AI and the moderating influence of digital culture climate. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on self-determination theory, the authors propose and empirically test a moderated mediation model using data collected from a three-wave, multisource survey of 298 employees working in three technology-oriented startups in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Structural equation modeling was used to examine the measurement and structural models and to test the hypothesized relationships among AI-enabled HR practices, trust in AI, digital culture climate and agile talent deployment. Findings Results reveal that AI-enabled HR practices positively influence agile talent deployment through increased employee trust in AI. In addition, the mediated relationship is stronger within organizations characterized by a robust digital culture climate, indicating that a digitally supportive organizational context enhances the effectiveness of AI-enabled HR initiatives. Originality/value The paper advances AI-enabled human resource management research by framing trust in AI as a mechanism translating supportive, transparent HR systems into agile talent deployment rather than technology acceptance. It identifies digital culture climate as an enactment condition enabling trust to become adaptive action. Practically, HR leaders should align explainable AI, trust-building practices and digital norms to strengthen workforce agility.

The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) demands innovative therapeutic strategies beyond conventional antibiotics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly those originating from the human, animal, and environmental microbiome, represent a promising frontier within public health microbiology and microbial food safety. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have revolutionized the discovery pipeline, enabling high-throughput mining of metagenomic data and de novo generation of novel peptide sequences. This perspective review synthesizes recent breakthroughs in AI-driven discovery of microbiome-originated AMPs, examines their preclinical efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens under One Health and climate-sensitive frameworks and application in infectious disease treatment and discusses translational challenges including pharmacokinetics, toxicity, manufacturing scalability, and applications in food preservation and water safety. We argue that the convergence of microbiome science, deep learning, and synthetic biology positions AI-discovered AMPs as viable next-generation interventions against antibiotic resistance across human, animal, and environmental domains.

Radiological examinations increasingly leverage artificial intelligence to enhance diagnostic performance by compensating for expertise shortages, particularly in specialized interpretation. Despite academic AI models achieving compelling accuracy, adoption remains low. An objective, evidence-based examination of AI-guided clinical image interpretation seeks to expose the underlying reasons. The primary challenge lies not in accuracy but in fully automated analysis, especially for multimodal and multidimensional datasets. Introduction of uncertainty measures, image explainability, and real-world data reduce recognition to a decisive-supporting role— helping radiologists to detect previously unnoticed abnormalities—or even to precautionary analysis. Patients requesting precision medicine and therapy planning—and those at high risk of neglected pathology—stand to gain the greatest benefit. Relevant AI architecture considers imaging cues suitable for precision medicine or requiring additional methods to obtain interpretable images. Successful performance testing against an external, hidden reference dataset promotes vital user trust. Machine learning achieves best results where all potentially pathological abnormalities are identified and their presence virtually guaranteed, as in multi-class recognition. Data scarcity, however, impedes clinically relevant solutions. Explainability, essential for medical applications and clinical acceptance, extends simply beyond clinical decision support to provide saliency maps and, better still, clinically meaningful image regions or qualities. Attention maps may even bring a form of rule-based reasoning within reach. Clinical integration that reproduces the technical conditions under which model diagnostic measures are calculated raises the challenge of uncertainty quantification—a necessary condition for clinical decision support. Convolutional neural networks trained for photo-quality classification, par excellence supervised image quality assessment, provide the basic cues for uncertainty quantification. Imaging acquisition, modality, and systems are also defined in terms of current PACS/EPIC systems. PE, pre-symptomatic examination or precautionary examination, is defined as a patientuser group prepared to cover the cost of an examination with lower diagnostic accuracy and a high level of uncertainty

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Salivary-gland biopsy is central to Sjögren’s disease (SjD) assessment, but conventional measures incompletely capture glandular heterogeneity. This systematic review evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) applications to SjD salivary-gland histopathology and molecular profiling, including biological and translational validation. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched. Eligible studies used salivary-gland tissue as the primary analytical substrate or provided substantive glandular validation of systemic AI/ML findings. Evidence was synthesized functionally because of methodological heterogeneity. Results: Twenty-five studies were included. AI/ML identified histopathological and molecular phenotypes spanning immune/interferon activation, tissue architecture and immune-cell organization, epithelial stress and metabolic/cell-death remodeling, and translational response. Only a limited subset progressed beyond computational or tissue-level confirmation to functional perturbation, pharmacological testing, in vivo validation, or human treatment-response assessment. Recurrent public-dataset reuse, small cohorts, heterogeneous pipelines, and limited independent validation constrained reproducibility. Conclusions: AI/ML supports multidimensional SjD glandular phenotyping and shows emerging translational potential, but demonstrated clinical or therapeutic utility remains unestablished. Prospective multicenter validation is required before AI-derived glandular phenotypes can inform routine patient stratification or therapeutic decision-making.
topics: Salivary Gland Tumors Diagnosis and Treatment

documents.abstract: This study presents the Forest Fire Rescue Decision Support System (FFR-DSS), an AI-powered framework integrating GPT-4-based semantic analysis with real-time Twitter data to support emergency rescue coordination during forest fires in Turkey. Using tweets from the catastrophic 2021 wildfires affecting Muğla and Antalya, FFR-DSS employs prompt-engineered large language model (LLM) pipelines to extract urgency scores, emotional tone, geographical information, and actionability indicators from crisis-related social media content. Unlike traditional natural language processing (NLP) approaches such as Bag-of-Words (BoW) and TF-IDF, which may struggle with contextually rich and emotionally variable messages, the proposed framework leverages GPT-4's zero-shot semantic reasoning capabilities without requiring task-specific labeled training datasets. A geospatial risk mapping component further aggregates tweet-level outputs into district-level risk scores and dynamic heatmaps, enabling emergency teams to identify critical areas and prioritize resource allocation. Evaluation against a manually annotated sample demonstrates that FFR-DSS achieves 92.4% classification precision and 89.1% recall, substantially outperforming the BoW+SVM baseline with 72.8% accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of LLM-augmented social media analytics to transform unstructured crisis communications into actionable intelligence, improving situational awareness, rescue coordination, and data-driven decision-making during large-scale natural disasters.In addition to its natural language understanding capabilities, FFR-DSS incorporates a geospatial mapping component to visualize and monitor critical rescue zones dynamically. By aligning semantic outputs with location data, the system helps authorities prioritize interventions in areas of greatest need. Empirical evaluations show that FFR-DSS achieves higher classification accuracy and interpretability than prior baseline methods, offering a more robust, transparent, and context-aware framework for emergency response. The results suggest that GPT-based systems represent a transformative step in disaster management technology, particularly in scenarios requiring rapid analysis and decision-making based on unstructured social media content.

Background and Objective: Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) present major challenges in clinical care, impacting patient safety and therapeutic outcomes. Traditional detection methods, often based on curated databases, may miss newly emerging interactions or require frequent manual updates. Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence (AI) offer novel tools for real-time, automated DDI detection directly from biomedical literature. This study introduces an AI-powered approach to identify DDIs, assign relevance scores to publications, and benchmark performance against conventional databases. Methods: We developed an NLP pipeline incorporating sentence classification to detect safety and interaction-related content, and named entity recognition (NER) to extract drug-drug interaction types, their clinical impact, and patient features. The sentence classification module is based on a BERT architecture fine-tuned from microsoft/BiomedNLP-BiomedBERT-baseuncased-abstract-fulltext, and the NER module uses the open-source model d4data/biomedical-ner-all. A DDI relevance score was designed to quantify each article’s significance based on weighted parameters derived from model outputs, with weights informed by domain experts (title relevance: 50 points, DDI impact: 40 points, publication type: 10 points). The system was validated on a manually curated dataset. We applied ANOVA and sensitivity analyses, and evaluated performance using recall, precision, and F1-score, comparing our method to established DDI resources. Key Content and Findings: The pipeline was validated on 7,751 articles across 15 query types. ROC analysis identified a relevance score threshold of 75%. Drug-family queries achieved the highest F1-score (0.872), followed by single-drug (0.731) and drug-drug queries (0.684). ANOVA and Tukey post-hoc analysis confirmed statistically significant differences in relevance scores between annotation groups (p < 0.05), with full stratification across all three groups for drug-drug family queries. Compared with manually compiled expert reference lists, our system retrieved substantially more relevant articles without requiring manual updates. Conclusion: AI-driven NLP approaches can enhance clinical decision support systems by providing comprehensive, evidence-based DDI detection and prioritization, offering scalable support for safer pharmacological decision-making. Keywords: Drug-drug Interactions; Natural Language Processing; Artificial Intelligence; Pharmacovigilance; Clinical Decision Support.

Abstract By enabling sentiment analysis, targeted advertising, automated moderation, tailored content recommendations, and generative content production, artificial intelligence (AI) has radically changed social media platforms. AI-powered social media has improved civic engagement, political communication, and public awareness, strengthening democratic participation. However, it has also brought about serious problems, such as deep fakes, algorithmic bias, political polarization, electoral manipulation, misinformation, and privacy threats. These trends have significant ramifications for electoral integrity, public trust, and democratic governance. This study looks at the advantages and disadvantages of AI-powered social media for democracy and makes policy suggestions for maintaining moral AI governance while defending democratic principles.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in the advertising industry, enabling brands to produce video content that is personalized, visually engaging, scalable, and cost‑effective. Despite these advantages, the proliferation of AI in advertising raises significant ethical concerns, particularly regarding authenticity, transparency, privacy, misinformation, and deepfakes. These issues are especially relevant among college students, who encounter advertisements extensively through social media platforms. This study investigates the perceptions of AI‑generated video advertisements among college students in Mumbai, with a focus on ethics, authenticity, and trust. A quantitative research design was employed, and primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered via Google Forms. The final sample consisted of 91 respondents, who provided insights into their social media usage, perceptions of AI‑driven advertising, and concerns related to ethical practices. The findings indicate that lack of transparency was the most prominent ethical concern (42%), followed by privacy misuse (30%) and misleading content or deepfakes (20%). Respondents emphasized the importance of clear disclosure of AI involvement, truthful communication, human oversight, protection of personal data, and avoidance of misleading or stereotypical representations. The study concludes that students do not categorically reject AI‑generated advertising; rather, their acceptance is contingent upon responsible and transparent application of AI technologies. Overall, the results highlight that technological innovation in advertising must be supported by authenticity, ethical communication, transparency, and human oversight to strengthen trust among college students in Mumbai. These insights contribute to ongoing debates on digital ethics and the responsible integration of AI in advertising practices. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI-Generated Video Advertisements, College Students, Advertising Ethics, Social Media
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This perspective paper reviews recent advancements and explores future, exciting opportunities for both artificial intelligence (AI)‐powered smart displays and AI‐assisted augmented reality (AR) eyeglasses. To begin, we analyze fundamental AI‐enhanced image‐quality techniques, including perceptual resolution upscaling algorithms, tone mapping, reverse tone mapping, and image‐quality analysis. Next, we examine the practical implementations of AI technologies for smart displays, in which both the visual experience and use case of novel display technologies can be improved. Finally, we further explore AI integration into wearable AR glasses, highlighting the enabled capabilities to improve display systems through waveguide combiner optimization and image correction, and exploring recent advances that go beyond color in AR glasses, such as eye tracking, foveated rendering, and physiological sensing. By outlining emerging trends and promising directions for next‐generation display technologies, this perspective will demonstrate the critical role of AI in enabling new capabilities, user experiences, and technological breakthroughs in the field of displays.

Urban air pollution is one of the most persistent environmental and public-health problems facing Indian cities, and Delhi in particular records some of the highest particulate matter concentrations in the world during the post-monsoon and winter months. Public air-quality portals in India largely display current or historical readings, but they rarely tell a city administrator what the air will look like over the next few days, or where a pollution spike is likely originating from. This gap between “knowing today's AQI” and “deciding what to do about it” motivates AirSense AI, a full-stack urban air-quality intelligence platform designed as an academic prototype for Delhi. The system ingests PM2.5, PM10 and NO₂ station readings together with weather variables, satellite fire detections and land-use information, converts pollutant concentrations into a standardized Air Quality Index using the U.S. EPA methodology, and applies a gradient-boosted decision tree model (XGBoost) to forecast AQI up to 72 hours ahead. In parallel, the platform combines NASA FIRMS active-fire data with OpenStreetMap land-use polygons and Haversine-distance calculations to rank probable pollution hotspots, and uses a large language model (Groq/LLaMA 3) to translate the resulting numerical evidence into readable, bilingual (English/Hindi) advisories and enforcement summaries for administrators and citizens. The results are presented through a React and Leaflet-based interactive dashboard. This paper describes the motivation, related work, and proposed architecture of AirSense AI as an integrated decision-support system rather than a monitoring-only tool. As the platform is at the prototype stage, no experimental forecasting accuracy, source-attribution validation, or user-study results are reported here; these are identified as required additions for the next version of this paper.

This study examines how algorithmic management in the gig economy is related to gig workers' workplace wellbeing. Specifically, we explore how algorithmic management corresponds with (positive) challenge appraisal and (negative) threat appraisal. We also examine the moderating role of psychological resilience in these relationships, as well as the implications of appraisal processes for workplace wellbeing. Data were collected from 389 food delivery workers in China. We find that algorithmic management is positively associated with both challenge appraisal and threat appraisal. Challenge appraisal is positively associated with workplace wellbeing, whereas threat appraisal is negatively associated with workplace wellbeing. Psychological resilience strengthens the challenge-appraisal pathway and the corresponding positive indirect relationship with workplace wellbeing, but it does not significantly buffer the threat-appraisal pathway. These findings show that algorithmic management is associated with both positive and negative appraisal processes and that psychological resilience may play different roles across these pathways. The study therefore offers a more nuanced explanation of the relationship between algorithmic management and gig workers' workplace wellbeing.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the demand for reliable, efficient, and interpretable machine learning (ML) methods for complex prediction and decision-making tasks. However, conventional ML approaches often encounter challenges related to model optimization, generalization, computational efficiency, data imbalance, and limited interpretability. This study proposes an Advanced Machine Learning Framework for Algorithm Development, Optimization, and Explainable Intelligent Prediction that integrates data preprocessing, feature engineering, algorithm selection, Hyperparameter optimization, ensemble learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Multiple ML algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, Gradient Boosting, and Extreme Gradient Boosting, are comparatively evaluated. Model performance is assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), computational efficiency, and interpretability. Furthermore, SHAP and LIME techniques are incorporated to explain feature contributions and improve transparency in model predictions. The framework facilitates systematic comparison between conventional and optimized models while examining the trade-off between predictive performance, computational cost, and explainability. The proposed approach provides a generalizable pathway for developing robust and trustworthy intelligent prediction systems. Its applicability extends across healthcare, education, cyber security, finance, and other data-driven domains. The study contributes an integrated framework that combines algorithmic optimization with explainability to support accurate, transparent, efficient, and reliable ML-based decision-making systems.
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Phenotyping is fundamental to rare disease diagnosis, but manually curating structured phenotypes from clinical notes is labor intensive and difficult to scale. Existing artificial intelligence (AI) approaches optimize individual components of phenotyping but generally do not operationalize the full workflow of extracting features from clinical text, standardizing them to Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, and prioritizing rare disease-relevant HPO terms. We developed RARE-PHENIX, an end-to-end AI framework for rare disease phenotyping that integrates large language model-based phenotype extraction, ontology-grounded standardization to HPO terms, and supervised ranking of HPO terms. We trained RARE-PHENIX using data from 2671 patients across 11 Undiagnosed Diseases Network clinical sites, and externally validated it on 16,357 real-world clinical notes from 143 patients at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Our findings suggest RARE-PHENIX generates structured, prioritized HPO terms highly concordant with clinician curation, demonstrates potential downstream disease-prioritization signal, and may support human-in-the-loop rare disease phenotyping in real-world settings.

documents.abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have had a substantial impact on software engineering research and practice, as well as on software engineering education. In Software Engineering (SE) education, prior studies have mainly examined students’ LLM usage through surveys, interviews, or short-term observations, offering limited visibility into their actual development activities. As a result, it remains unclear how students’ perceptions of LLM usage match their actual development practices. To address this gap, we analyze course project data collected over three years from 158 students enrolled in an upper-level SE course, together with students’ experience-sharing presentations, survey responses, and activity logs. We examine LLM integration by jointly analyzing students’ perceived usage and usefulness from surveys and presentations, their actual development activities captured through VS Code activity logs, and their project performance based on evaluation results across different levels of LLM support. By combining these analyses, we connect students’ reported LLM usage with their actual development activities and assess its relation to learning outcomes in SE course projects. Our results show that students utilized LLMs frequently for code-related tasks and generally found them helpful, with frequent usage increasing over the course project while perceptions shifted as project complexity grew. Activity log analysis revealed divergent patterns in LLM usage, reflecting both increasing dependency and deliberate efforts to maintain development independence. Across three years, integrating LLM support did not lead to statistically significant differences in final project achievement as measured by requirement satisfaction, although students with LLM support produced substantially larger software systems and lower-performing teams showed mild benefits, suggesting that LLMs may help reduce the influence of programming proficiency on project outcomes. Our findings highlight both the benefits and tensions of LLM integration in SE course projects and suggest that future SE course designs may incorporate more complex and challenging SE tasks beyond implementation-focused requirements, while also providing explicit education on prompt engineering, supporting students’ code comprehension of rapidly generated LLM-assisted code, and helping students avoid excessive dependency on LLM tools during development.

Title Anatomical target and guidance technique for cervical medial branch block: a systematic review and meta-analysis of targeting accuracy and diagnostic yield 1、Registration status This registration is submitted retrospectively. Protocol development began before the searches reported below were executed. At the time of registration on 15 October 2026, the following activities had already been completed: database searching (Europe PMC, OpenAlex, VIP, ClinicalTrials.gov), title and abstract screening, full-text retrieval for 62 records, data extraction from the included cohorts, and the primary meta-analysis. Registration was delayed because the review was initiated as an internal evidence synthesis and the decision to prepare it for publication was made only after the analyses had been run. A later registration cannot establish that the methodological decisions were pre-specified. 2、Background Neck pain is among the most prevalent musculoskeletal complaints worldwide. A substantial proportion of cases arise from the cervical zygapophysial (facet) joints, with controlled diagnostic studies estimating a prevalence of 36% to 67%. Because clinical examination cannot reliably identify this source, diagnosis depends on image-guided blockade of the medial branch nerves. The technical elements of the procedure (anatomical target, guidance modality, confirmatory tool, and injectate volume) are inconsistently defined, and their influence on targeting accuracy, block positivity, and safety has not been synthesised. 3、Review question In adults with chronic neck pain or cervicogenic headache of suspected cervical facet joint origin, how do anatomical target definitions and guidance or confirmation techniques for cervical medial branch block affect targeting accuracy, block diagnostic yield, and safety? 4、Eligibility criteria Included: original studies of any design (randomised trials, prospective and retrospective cohorts, cross-sectional studies, diagnostic accuracy studies, case series with at least five participants); adults aged 18 years or older with chronic neck pain and/or cervicogenic headache undergoing cervical medial branch block or facet joint block; studies reporting block-level outcomes (targeting accuracy, technical success, block positivity rate, or comparisons of target definitions, guidance modalities, or patient-selection strategies); cadaveric and anatomical studies reporting human target accuracy (analysed separately); publication from 2015 onwards. Excluded: studies reporting only post-radiofrequency outcomes without block-level data; systematic reviews, narrative reviews, study protocols, editorials, and case reports; studies of the thoracic, lumbar, or sacral regions; studies without extractable quantitative data. 5、Outcomes Primary: proportion of patients achieving at least 50% pain relief after cervical medial branch block or radiofrequency procedures, at three months or later. Secondary: technical success and targeting accuracy according to the definition used by each study; block positivity rate at thresholds of 50% and 80% relief; complications and adverse events, including intravascular injection; false-positive and false-negative rates against subsequent radiofrequency outcome. 6、Search strategy Searched resources: Europe PMC (indexing MEDLINE/PubMed), OpenAlex, VIP, and the ClinicalTrials.gov registry; reference lists and citations of included studies and relevant previous reviews were screened. Search period 2015 onwards. Search terms combined population terms (cervical, neck pain, cervicogenic, whiplash, cervical facet) with intervention terms (medial branch, facet joint block, facet block, zygapophysial). Resources not searched: Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, ProQuest, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL, Wanfang, SinoMed, and the WHO ICTRP registry could not be searched because the subscription proxy service used for these resources was non-functional throughout the review period. OpenAlex was used as an additional bibliographic index to partially compensate; it is not equivalent to a curated citation database. 7、Study selection and data extraction Titles, abstracts, and full texts were screened against the eligibility criteria by one investigator and an AI-assisted screening tool independently, with disagreements resolved by discussion. A calibration exercise on 25 records preceded formal screening (human-AI agreement 81.8%, kappa 0.58). Data were extracted with a standardised form covering study identifiers, design, population, cervical levels, target definition, guidance modality, needle approach, confirmatory tool, injectate and volume, and outcome definitions with numerators and denominators. All values were verified against source full texts. 8、Risk of bias and certainty of evidence Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for non-randomised studies, RoB 2 for randomised trials, and QUADAS-2 or a study-specific checklist for diagnostic accuracy and cadaveric studies. Certainty of evidence was assessed with GRADE, starting at low for observational designs. 9、Data synthesis Proportions were pooled using a random-intercepts logistic model with logit transformation, maximum likelihood estimation of tau-squared, and the Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Heterogeneity was quantified with tau-squared, I-squared, and Cochran Q. Pre-specified subgroup analyses compared radiofrequency versus block procedures, guidance modality, injectate volume, confirmatory tool, and follow-up duration. Leave-one-out analysis was performed for the primary outcome and the subgroup comparison. Publication bias was not assessed because of the small number of studies per outcome. Safety outcomes were summarised descriptively rather than pooled, because of extreme imbalance in study size across cohorts. Analyses used R 4.6.1 with the meta package. 10、Expected outcomes / dissemination The review will quantify the proportion of patients achieving meaningful pain relief after cervical medial branch procedures, describe technical success according to the definition used, and summarise the safety profile. It will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal (target: Medicine (Baltimore)). The registration number and DOI will be cited in the final article.

With the advent of Covid-19, it is necessary to repurpose new treatment alternatives, either in the form of an effective single dose of these antidiabetic drug agents or an efficacious combination of them for elderly population with or had suffered this condition. Newer medication classes for diabetes have been increasing in use, and their utilization varied across provinces and how the COVID-19 pandemic may have affected these trends. This mini review has the objective of predicting the targets of bioactive small molecules in human using healthcare applied artificial intelligence. These substances in the body are target specific receptors on the surface of cells, and antidiabetic drugs contains moiety´s and functional groups that may act on one or several subtypes of receptors. The tool is a tuned algorithm, with novel data bank in web interface. Information figures of Swiss Target Prediction (STP), which allow predictions on therapy combinations and probable side effects, were reordered. The bibliographic databases were searched to identify existing cost studies, economic evaluations and models, and most of the parameters were derived from the published literatura. Predictions are done using a ligand-based approach, based on the similarity between a query molecule and the known ligands of a large collection of protein targets. The result of this study highlighted crucial recommendations for the use of some of the antidiabetic agent groups in diabetic patients. Our findings provide real world evidence supporting the potential clinical benefits of diabetes drug agents in mitigating side effects and development in patients with T2DM.

Background: Anxiety has been increasingly recognized as a relevant contributor to cardiometabolic dysfunction through neuroendocrine, inflammatory, and behavioral mechanisms. However, evidence evaluating the relationship between anxiety symptoms, lifestyle habits, and cardiometabolic risk in large occupational populations remains limited. This study aimed to analyze the association between Goldberg Anxiety and Depression Scale (GADS) scores, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic risk factors in a large cohort of Spanish workers. Methods: A cross-sectional observational study was conducted in 119,336 Spanish workers undergoing routine occupational health examinations between 2021 and 2023. Anxiety symptoms were assessed using the GADS. Lifestyle variables included smoking status, physical activity assessed with the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ), and adherence to the Mediterranean diet evaluated through the Prevention with Mediterranean Diet (PREDIMED) questionnaire. Anthropometric measurements, blood pressure, lipid profile, fasting glucose, obesity, abdominal obesity, and metabolic syndrome were analyzed. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (ORs) for cardiometabolic abnormalities according to anxiety status and lifestyle factors. Results: Elevated GADS scores were significantly associated with worse cardiometabolic profiles in both sexes, including higher blood pressure, triglycerides, fasting glucose, body mass index, waist circumference, and lower high-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentrations. Workers with elevated anxiety presented markedly higher prevalences of hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, impaired fasting glucose, abdominal obesity, and metabolic syndrome (all p < 0.001). After multivariable adjustment, elevated anxiety remained independently associated with hypertension (OR 6.48; 95% confidence interval (CI) 5.89– 7.09), hypertriglyceridemia (OR 5.31; 95% CI 4.60–6.02), and impaired fasting glucose (OR 5.23; 95% CI 4.64–5.83). Physical inactivity and low adherence to the Mediterranean diet were associated with a less favorable cardiometabolic profile among participants with elevated anxiety scores. Elevated GADS scores were independently associated with all major cardiometabolic outcomes after multivariable adjustment, with the strongest associations observed for hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, and impaired fasting glucose. Conclusions: Elevated GADS scores are strongly associated with adverse cardiometabolic profiles in Spanish workers, particularly when combined with unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. These findings support the integration of mental health assessment and lifestyle interventions into occupational cardiometabolic prevention strategies.

Abstract: Climate change, population growth, and increasing pressure on natural resources pose major challenges to global agricultural production. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising technology for addressing these challenges through precision farming, machine learning, robotic automation, and data-driven decision-making. This study examines the applications of AI in crop management, real-time monitoring, yield prediction, resource optimization, and sustainable agricultural production. The integration of AI with advanced genetic technologies can improve productivity, resource-use efficiency, and climate resilience. However, challenges related to technology, infrastructure, farmer awareness, data availability, affordability, and regulatory frameworks limit its widespread adoption. The study highlights the need for supportive policies, capacity building, digital infrastructure, and collaboration among farmers, researchers, industries, and policymakers. Overall, AI has significant potential to transform modern agriculture, enhance food security, and promote sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural development.

ABSTRACT Accurate and scalable evaluation of gene‐editing efficiency is crucial for the development of novel editing tools. However, conventional methods are laborious, costly, and low‐throughput. Here, we developed an artificial intelligence (AI)‐driven fluorescent reporter (AR) platform, an integrated system that automates and streamlines the entire evaluation workflow. The AR platform combines an enhanced fluorescent reporter with an AI‐driven analytical pipeline. The dual‐fluorescence reporter system, in which mCherry carrying a PEST domain is paired with GFP, supports Cas variants with diverse PAM requirements and quantifies editing efficiency as the proportion of GFP‐only cells. The platform's AI module, EasyReporter, integrates a deep learning model for automated cell segmentation and quantification with a large language model (LLM)‐based agent for intelligent data interpretation and comprehensive report generation. Editing efficiencies measured by AR correlated with those measured by flow cytometry (Spearman ρ = 0.77) and amplicon sequencing (Spearman ρ = 0.83). The AR platform provides a high‐throughput and automated workflow that accelerates gene‐editing research. In the future, it will be particularly effective for quantifying the efficiency of large‐fragment gene editing, offering a new framework for AI‐empowered biological laboratories.

Scientific papers keep much of their quantitative content in tables and supplementary files, where a number means something only through its header, caption, unit, analytical method, and the conventions of its field. Recovering the rows and columns of a table is therefore not the same as recovering the scientific fact it reports. Most semantic table-interpretation methods assume that a clean table is already available and subsequently map its cells or columns to ontology terms, whereas most publication-level extraction systems are designed for a single domain. We study a middle path: a shared process that reads a paper and its supplementary files, gathers evidence from several parsers and a language model, and reconciles that evidence, while a bounded human-authored task module for each task supplies the domain meaning. The module lists the canonical names the graph may use, the surface forms that map to them, a small set of derivation rules and validity constraints, an identity key, and the bindings used to write RDF. It defines what a task is allowed to emit; it does not try to list every convention of a field. We build four such modules (for drug-discovery chemistry, materials science, machine learning, and mineral geochemistry) in the ArticleMiner framework, and evaluate them on 163 papers, including a new geochemistry benchmark with expert-curated ground truth. In comparisons against a same-LLM few-shot baseline, the point estimates favor ArticleMiner on all four tasks, with uncertainty on the two smaller benchmarks. The geochemistry comparison also includes access to supplementary files, so its improvement cannot be attributed to domain guidance alone.

Abstract Musculoskeletal care is being reshaped by population aging, multimorbidity, frailty, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, polypharmacy and increasing vulnerability to postoperative loss of independence. Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered orthopaedic research, but its clinical translation remains constrained. Many models address isolated diagnostic, imaging or short‐term prediction tasks rather than the longitudinal care trajectories that determine outcomes in older musculoskeletal patients. The central limitation is therefore not simply whether older adults are represented in datasets, but whether AI systems are valid across the continuum of geriatric orthopaedic care. This review argues for a transition from task‐specific orthopaedic AI toward continuum‐of‐care AI for the aging musculoskeletal patient. Upstream, radiomics, longitudinal osteoarthritis phenotyping, opportunistic computed tomography (CT)‐based skeletal assessment and AI‐augmented dual‐energy X‐ray absorptiometry (DXA) modelling may improve prediction of disease progression, fracture risk, treatment failure and surgical timing. At the point of intervention, AI‐assisted arthroplasty planning may help move total knee arthroplasty from generic alignment targets toward phenotype‐specific reconstruction strategies that account for constitutional alignment, bone morphology, ligament envelope, neuromuscular control, frailty and functional reserve. Perioperatively, automated frailty and sarcopenia phenotyping, wearable gait analysis and multimodal temporal models integrating imaging, electronic health records, laboratory data, medications, patient‐reported outcomes and wearable signals may support dynamic risk prediction. After discharge, continuous monitoring of mobility, sleep, pain trajectories, wound‐related symptoms and rehabilitation adherence may help close the high‐risk surveillance gap during the 90‐day postoperative episode. However, clinical adoption requires more than high discrimination. Explainable AI should be understood as one component of a broader trust framework that also includes calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision‐curve analysis, external and prospective validation, workflow integration, post‐deployment monitoring and accountability. The future of orthopaedic AI is not simply better diagnosis or more precise surgery, but longitudinal, multimodal support across the full care continuum: predicting progression, selecting treatment, personalizing surgery, optimizing perioperative care, monitoring recovery and preserving mobility and independence. Level of Evidence Level IV.

documents.abstract: Recent dynamic advances in AI technologies have brought about profound transformations in the marketing paradigm and in consumer behavior and interactions. At the heart of this transformation, the relationship between AI agents and consumer behavior stands out as a timely area calling for in-depth investigation in the literature. This study constitutes a bibliometric analysis undertaken to reveal the intellectual accumulation of knowledge in this conceptual domain and to examine the evolution of the literature systematically. To this end, 438 articles indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database between 2020 and 2026 were subjected to a comprehensive examination. The research first conducted a performance analysis to resolve the quantitative structure of the field, mapping annual publication distributions, the most prolific authors, the most highly cited studies, leading countries, and institutional collaborations. It then carried out citation, co-citation, and co-occurence analyses using science mapping techniques in order to structure the intellectual framework of the field. The findings show that the AI agent literature emerging in the context of consumer behavior is following a growth trend that is gaining momentum in both quantitative and qualitative terms. Thematically, the literature was found to concentrate on the transparency and interpretability of AI algorithms, the implications of these algorithms for consumer attitudes and behavior, the strengthening of human-AI interaction through anthropomorphic design elements, the dark side encompassing ethics, privacy, and trust, and sectoral reflections in the service industry.

documents.abstract: Abstract Weed infestation is a persistent constraint on the cultivation of medicinal and aromatic crops, reducing yield, quality consistency, raw-material safety, and production standardization. Although herbicide-based weed management has improved labor efficiency, increasing concerns over pesticide residues, herbicide resistance, crop selectivity, and ecological impacts limit its suitability for high-quality herbal medicine production. This review synthesizes the evolution of weed control in medicinal crop systems from manual and mechanical practices to chemical control, integrated weed management, and emerging intelligent–ecological strategies. We propose the concept of Weed Control 4.0 as a crop-specific framework that combines artificial intelligence, intelligent machinery, bioherbicides, and ecological regulation. The review summarizes how microbial and plant-derived bioherbicides suppress weeds through growth inhibition, allelopathic interference, pathogen-mediated damage, and disruption of weed physiological metabolism. It further discusses how machine vision, sensor fusion, robotic platforms, precision spraying, and data-driven decision support can enable real-time weed identification and site-specific intervention. Ecological approaches, including crop rotation, intercropping, mulching, cover crops, allelopathic crops, beneficial insects, and soil microbial manipulation, are evaluated for their potential to suppress weed communities while maintaining soil health and agroecosystem stability. Finally, we identify key challenges for implementation, including medicinal crop-specific weed databases, biosafety and efficacy evaluation of bioherbicides, integration of field machinery with agronomic practices, and residue-safe regulatory standards. Weed Control 4.0 offers a pathway toward sustainable, precise, and residue-safe weed management for the standardized production of high-quality herbal medicines.

This text starts from an AI error incident of September 2026 within US Special Operations Command that ‘almost started a war’. It examines the growing significance of ‘Human Factors’ in European defence as artificial intelligence reshapes relations between humans, military institutions and technological systems. Drawing on European Defence Agency programmes and recent work on trustworthy AI, I suggest that AI changes where and how humans enter military systems, embedding them in increasingly complex sociotechnical relations. Human capacities themselves start to acquire an infrastructural quality, as military systems depend increasingly on how these capacities are organized and managed.

Empirical evidence on how artificial intelligence (AI) relates to student engagement in culturally diverse higher-education settings remains limited. In Chinese university classrooms, where interaction is often teacher-led and asking questions in class can carry a social cost, AI-driven dialogic tools may offer low-pressure opportunities for active participation. This study examined the association between an AI conversational agent (EduBot) and the behavioural, cognitive, emotional and agentic dimensions of engagement among Chinese undergraduates. A mixed-methods quasi-experimental design involved 555 students in four comprehensive (multi-disciplinary, research-intensive) universities, each contributing one introductory course taught in two parallel sections. Within a 15-week semester, intervention sections (n = 278) used EduBot, a Socratic-dialogue agent embedded in the learning management system, for 12 weeks; control sections (n = 277) used teaching-assistant-moderated forums. We measured engagement at three time points with a 21-item four-dimensional engagement scale adapted from an established measure and supplemented it with system logs, 30 student interviews and instructor focus groups. Linear mixed-effects models accounting for the nesting of students within course sections, together with mixed-design ANOVAs, showed Group × Time interactions for behavioural (η 2 p = 0.043, post-test d = 0.71), cognitive (η 2 p = 0.032, d = 0.55), agentic (η 2 p = 0.054, d = 0.57) and emotional engagement (η 2 p = 0.012, d = 0.34), all p ≤ 0.001 after Holm adjustment. Within the intervention group, the number of EduBot sessions predicted post-test engagement after adjustment for baseline scores and covariates. Exploratory moderation analyses indicated larger agentic gains among first-year students and larger cognitive gains among students with lower prior GPA. Thematic analysis identified three hypothesised mechanisms, namely a judgment-free interaction space, scaffolded persistence and temporal flexibility. A Socratic-scaffolded AI agent was associated with higher engagement, most clearly for agentic engagement, which participants described as constrained by classroom norms. The findings support culturally attentive AI design and suggest, tentatively, an equity-enhancing potential. Because the design compared an integrated AI package with usual practice across eight sections, the effects cannot be attributed to single design components.

documents.abstract: Background: Stem cell bioprocessing requires timely assessment of cell state and control over variable expansion and differentiation. Automated culture can execute predefined steps, whereas adaptive manufacturing uses observations to guide decisions during an ongoing batch.Objective: This review examines how artificial intelligence and machine learning connect process monitoring to prediction and feedback control, and assesses which links have been demonstrated in stem cell systems.Key Content: This topic covers image-based phenotyping, physical and multimodal sensing, growth and differentiation forecasts, process optimization, hybrid models, and proposed digital twins. A descriptive Level 0–6 continuum distinguishes endpoint assessment, monitoring, state estimation, prediction, operator decision support, within-run feedback, and coordinated workflow autonomy. Reported studies demonstrate image-guided adjustments to differentiation, robotic optimization across experiments, and rule-based feedback within a culture. However, these capabilities do not demonstrate autonomous production of a clinically releasable cell product. Translation is further limited by reduced model performance when entire experiments are withheld from training, fragmented datasets, variation across donors and processes, uncertain links between surrogate measures and potency, and the need for model governance.Conclusion: Supervised adaptation and supervised autonomy are credible near-term targets, characterized by bounded, traceable interventions with human oversight and a defined response to uncertainty. Prospective studies should compare adaptive and fixed processes across independent batches and assess cell identity, relevant function, safety-related attributes, and resource use. Claims of full autonomy require verified performance across the manufacturing workflow.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a change agent in healthcare and promises to change clinical decision-making opportunities.AI can be used in nursing to increase efficiency, minimize human error, and support evidence-based practice, among other things.Nevertheless, the attitudes, awareness, and desire of nurses to implement AI are still crucial prerequisites to effective integration into clinical processes.Purpose: This research targeted the awareness, perceived advantages, difficulties, and attitudes of nurses to AI as a decision-making tool and determined the reliability and validity of the tool applied.To add to that, the research has also investigated the effects of demographic characteristics like gender, education, and workplace on perceptions and readiness to embrace AI.Methods: A cross-sectional survey design was used, where 237 nurses in 9 hospitals, clinics, community care, and academic institutions were surveyed to gather data.The Likert scale questions (Q620) included in the structured type of questionnaire were demographic data.We used statistical analysis, which is the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, Cronbach's Alpha reliability, KMO, and Bartlett test of validity, independent sampling t-test, one-way ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis test, Chi-square test, Pearson correlation, and regression analysis.Findings: The data were normally distributed (p > 0.05), and the reliability (Cronbach's Alpha = 0.92) was excellent, as well as the validity (KMO = 0.82; Bartlett's p = 0.001).Cross-group comparisons demonstrated that there was a high level of difference by gender, education, and workplace, and the chi-square analysis indicated that education and AI training were strongly correlated.Pearson correlation also revealed positive relationships between all items in the questionnaire, which showed that there was coherence between awareness, perceived benefits, and adoption.Regression analysis found awareness and understanding to have a strong positive influence on willingness to adopt AI, with age playing a positive but insignificant role.Conclusion: The research concludes that the willingness of nurses to embrace AI is majorly dependent on their awareness and knowledge of the technology, with the educational and workplace context

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the nature, methods, and applications of geographical research. The integration of AI with Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Remote Sensing, Global Positioning Systems (GPS), and geospatial big data has created new opportunities for analyzing complex spatial and temporal processes. This study examines the evolving relationship between Artificial Intelligence and Geography, with particular emphasis on its applications, transformative potential, limitations, and future possibilities. The study adopts a descriptive, analytical, and exploratory approach based primarily on secondary data obtained from research articles, academic publications, institutional reports, and relevant scholarly literature. It examines the application of AI across major geographical domains, including Physical Geography, Human Geography, Urban Geography, and Economic Geography. The findings indicate that AI enhances geographical research through automated spatial analysis, image classification, predictive modelling, environmental monitoring, disaster prediction, urban planning, and data-driven decision-making. However, challenges related to data quality, algorithmic bias, transparency, privacy, technological dependence, and unequal access to digital infrastructure remain significant. The study argues that AI should not be viewed as a replacement for geographical expertise but as a complementary technological capability. The future of Geography is therefore likely to be shaped by human–AI collaboration, integrating computational intelligence with geographical reasoning, field knowledge, contextual understanding, and ethical judgement to address emerging spatial and environmental challenges

Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally transforming investment strategies by enabling data-driven decision-making, behavioural insights, and adaptive portfolio management. This chapter examines the evolving role of AI in financial markets by integrating theoretical perspectives, including market efficiency and behavioural finance, with emerging empirical evidence. It explores the growing importance of big data, algorithmic trading, and AI-driven sentiment analysis in shaping market dynamics. The study further analyzes adaptive portfolio strategies, highlighting the role of machine learning and robo-advisory platforms in enhancing efficiency and personalization. In addition, it addresses key regulatory, ethical, and governance challenges, including algorithmic transparency, data privacy, and systemic risk. Through case-based insights, the chapter identifies both opportunities and limitations of AI adoption. It concludes by emphasizing the need for responsible innovation, human AI collaboration, and robust policy frameworks to ensure sustainable and inclusive financial markets.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are transforming the productive core of the global economy, yet public debate remains dominated by single-number claims about the proportion of jobs “at risk”—claims that collapse heterogeneous technologies, tasks, and adoption conditions into a single misleading index. This thesis develops, verifies, and applies a multidimensional framework for assessing the employment consequences of AI and automation across economic sectors. The framework distinguishes four constructs that previous research has often conflated: (D1) digital AI exposure, defined as the proportion of a sector’s task content that current AI systems can technically support or perform; (D2) physical automation, defined as the automatable share of embodied, manual tasks; (D3) adoption, defined as the actual, observed deployment of AI and automation technologies within a sector; and (D4) net employment impact, defined as the estimated medium-term effect on total employment after accounting for displacement, reinstatement, and the creation of new tasks. The thesis proceeds in four stages. First, it reconstructs the technical foundations of machine learning, generative models, and robotics with sufficient rigor for economic analysis, while tracing the economic theory of technology-induced labor reallocation from Ricardo’s machinery question to the contemporary task-based literature. Second, it formalizes the four-dimensional framework through explicit index definitions, aggregation functions, and uncertainty treatment, deriving each dimension from documented methodologies, including task-exposure assessments, adoption surveys, and causal labor-market studies. Third, it applies the framework to nine sectors: information technology, finance and insurance, healthcare, education, manufacturing, construction, transportation and logistics, hospitality and food services, and retail and e-commerce. This analysis synthesizes approximately 280 verified sources, including causal evidence on industrial robots, randomized evaluations of generative AI assistants, and institutional data on technology adoption. Fourth, it examines the implications of the findings, demonstrating that sector-level net employment effects are mediated more strongly by adoption frictions, complementarities, and institutional conditions than by raw technical exposure alone. Employment effects are distributed unevenly across sectors and occupations rather than being confined to aggregate outcomes, and policy interventions can influence outcomes along all four dimensions. Methodologically, the thesis is grounded in a systematic review protocol with preregistered inclusion criteria, a two-pass, point-by-point verification of every citation, reference, and internal cross-reference, and an automated consistency audit whose results are reported in full. Its central conclusion is that a one-size-fits-all approach is inadequate: accurately assessing the labor-market consequences of AI requires keeping the four dimensions analytically distinct, because technologies with identical exposure profiles can produce opposing employment outcomes under different adoption conditions and institutional arrangements. The thesis concludes with scenario analyses for 2035 and a policy agenda addressing education, social protection, taxation, competition, and AI governance.
