documents.abstract: BEYOND AUTOMATION: INVESTIGATING THE INFLUENCE OF COGNITIVE BIASES ON HUMAN INTERPRETATION OF EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE PROF(DR.) VIJAYKUMAR B GADHAVI PROFESSOR AND HEAD , SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY, SWARRNIM START-UP AND INNOVATION UNIVERSITY - GANDHINAGAR GUJARAT INDIA ORCID: 0009-0005-6313-5900, E-MAIL: DRVIJAYKUMAR@SWARRNIM.EDU.IN PARMAR JIGAR JAYSUKHBHAI B. TECH. CE STUDENT, SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY SWARRNIM STARTUP & INNOVATION UNIVERSITY, GANDHINAGAR, GUJARAT, INDIA ORCID: 0009-0008-7651-9913, EMAIL: JIGARAHIR410@GMAIL.COM Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is intended to make algorithmic outputs more understandable, auditable, and contestable. Yet an explanation does not reach a neutral observer: people interpret it through prior beliefs, cognitive shortcuts, professional experience, and assumptions about machine competence. This conceptual paper examines how cognitive biases shape the interpretation of XAI and why greater transparency does not necessarily produce better decisions. Drawing on research on automation bias, judgment and decision-making, explainability, and human–AI collaboration, the paper develops an integrative framework linking explanation characteristics, user cognition, task context, and reliance behavior. It argues that anchoring, confirmation bias, availability, authority effects, and cognitive miserliness can transform explanations into persuasive cues rather than evidence for independent evaluation. Explanations may improve mental models and error detection when they are faithful, appropriately scoped, and matched to users’ needs; however, they may also legitimize an incorrect prediction, increase cognitive load, or create an illusion of understanding. The paper proposes design principles centered on calibrated trust, contrastive and uncertainty-aware explanations, independent judgment, verification prompts, and evaluation of decision quality rather than satisfaction alone. Because this is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, its propositions require experimental testing across domains and user groups. The central conclusion is that responsible XAI must design not only for model transparency but also for the cognitive conditions under which people interpret explanations. Keywords: explainable artificial intelligence, cognitive bias, automation bias, human–AI interaction, trust calibration, decision-making, algorithmic transparency
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Microalgae and cyanobacteria are valuable sources of bioactive ingredients and innovative biological systems for skin applications. Their metabolites include exopolysaccharides (EPS), mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs), carotenoids, phycobiliproteins, peptides and lipopeptides, polyunsaturated lipids, chlorophyll derivatives, and distinctive secondary metabolites such as scytonemin. Cyanobacteria additionally provide defined molecular candidates, including sacran, C-phycocyanin, MAAs, scytonemin-related compounds, and specialized peptide scaffolds. These compounds may support hydration and barrier function, photoprotection, control of oxidative stress and inflammation, pigmentation, antimicrobial and antibiofilm activity, extracellular-matrix preservation, and wound repair. This review examines major bioactive families, their sources and mechanisms, with particular emphasis on the strength of evidence supporting skin applications. Recent developments from 2024 to 2026 are highlighted, including microalgal extracellular vesicles (nanoalgosomes), photoactivated antimicrobial systems, photosynthetic hydrogels and microneedle patches, green extraction and biorefinery strategies, reconstructed human skin and skin-on-chip models, and artificial-intelligence-assisted formulation. Most reported effects remain supported mainly by biochemical, cellular, or preclinical evidence, whereas human validation is still limited. Translation will, therefore, depend on rigorous chemical standardization, effective cutaneous delivery, demonstrated stability and safety, scalable manufacturing, and validation in human-relevant models. Microalgae and cyanobacteria thus extend beyond conventional natural extracts toward next-generation dermocosmetic and cutaneous-delivery platforms.

Digital Islamic learning presents challenges involving unverified religious claims, artificial intelligence outputs, privacy concerns, and unequal access. This study aims to reconstruct the philosophy of ta’dib as a conceptual foundation for character education in digitally mediated Islamic learning. It employs a qualitative conceptual approach through purposive document analysis and an integrative synthesis of literature on educational philosophy and digital ethics. The findings propose the Ta’dib-Oriented Digital Character Pedagogy (TDCP) model, comprising five dimensions: epistemic integrity, dignified interaction, responsible digital agency, equitable participation, and reflective self-discipline. These dimensions are implemented through a cycle of inquiry, deliberation, action, and reflection to support formative assessment and protect learner privacy. The model offers a pedagogical framework for developing ethical reasoning without equating observable behavior with piety. Expert validation and empirical testing are needed to assess its applicability in educational settings.

As heritage tourism expands and shifts toward experience-oriented models, understanding how ritualized host–guest interaction generates meaning and contributes to value co-creation has become crucial. This study explores the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which ritualized host–guest interaction influences value co-creation behavior. Based on three scenario-based experiments and a field quasi-experiment at a heritage destination, it proposes and empirically tests a pathway linking interaction, cognition, trust, and value co-creation. The results show that heritage cognition and host–guest trust serve as dual mediators, illustrating the intertwined process of cognitive meaning-making and social relationship formation embedded in ritualized encounters. Furthermore, cultural salience shows a directional tendency to attenuate the cognitive pathway linking ritualized interaction to heritage cognition, while place attachment strengthens the trust-based pathway leading to value co-creation. The field quasi-experiment further supports the ecological validity of the proposed model. This study expands the social-psychological understanding of ritual in tourism and advances theoretical insights into how cultural experiences are transformed into value co-creation behavior. The findings offer practical implications for heritage destination management by emphasizing ritual-based design, cognitive engagement, and affective bonding as key drivers of heritage tourism development.

AI agents now run Earth observation (EO) workflows end to end, and their authors judge them on the task: answer accuracy, tool use, report scores and case studies. None of these evaluations asks whether the agent acted on a bad input. We ran five published EO and climate agents (LLM-Geo, Earth-Agent, WildfireGPT, ClimSight and PangaeaGPT) on their authors' own example tasks, and all five solved them on correct data. We then corrupted one input per system with a fault any expert would reject at a glance: impossible values (land at −267 °C, a July of 86.77 °C, 35 °C in Arctic water) or the wrong place (Tennessee census tracts for a North Carolina task, a wildfire site in the open Atlantic). Across 106 runs, scored on what reached the user, 85 used the bad data and said nothing, 4 said the data were wrong, and 17 changed what they delivered. In several runs the agent's own trace shows it noticed the problem and delivered an answer anyway. The faults are defined against four checks an expert applies to EO data: Validity, Fit, Uncertainty and Compliance. This study tests the first two. We propose evaluating EO agents by corrupting their data on purpose, reading the trace, and scoring what the agent did about the fault. Poster presented at the BIFOLD-ESA Workshop "Agentic AI for Earth Observation", Berlin, 19 October 2026.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Learning analytics has been increasingly using predictive models to support educational decision-making. However, the trade-off between predictive accuracy and interpretability remains a central challenge that limits how these models can be understood and used by educators. This study examines grey-box approaches to performance prediction by comparing two strategies: a theory-driven approach that groups interaction data into pedagogically meaningful categories, and a data-driven approach based on raw clickstream events followed by post hoc eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques. Using clickstream data from three educational contexts with different scales and instructional formats, we empirically compare the predictive performance, interpretability, and pedagogical relevance of both strategies. The results show that raw-event models achieve higher predictive performance in the large-scale online context with rich interaction data, where XAI methods provide relatively stable and consistent explanatory patterns. In the smaller-scale blended setting, where platform data capture only part of the learning activity, theory-driven aggregation provides a predictive advantage, although results become inconclusive in very small cohorts. The findings indicate that there is no single optimal approach, and that modeling strategies should be selected according to data characteristics, instructional design, and analytic goals. From a human-centered learning analytics perspective, the study highlights the importance of methodological alignment for the meaningful and responsible use of predictive models in education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: In this chapter, the researchers explore how women can be empowered through the deployment of sophisticated technologies, specifically artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and digital entrepreneurship, in relation to sustainable development. The study will focus on the ways that these digital tools can facilitate gender equality by increasing access to education, economic opportunities, and governance among women and also combat persistent challenges that may affect them, including digital divide, algorithmic bias, and under-representation in digital technology design. The systematic narrative review approach was used, which implies more than 40 published studies within the period of 2019-2025 as the sources to be analyzed and obtained via prominent academic databases. The research establishes that, despite the fact that the use of ICTs (information and communication technologies) have significantly enhanced socioeconomic mobility among women, issues like affordability, digital illiteracy, and sociocultural biases still limit full participation. It is important to note that the potential of AI is hindered by the gender biases inherent in the design of algorithms and that the IoT technologies, even though focusing on women and their safety in business ventures, do not have gender inclusion in their development. Furthermore, the idea of smart cities and e-governance systems have potentials of improving the agency of women in politics, but it needs to be more advanced to ensure it is more inclusive. The chapter highlights the need to have gender-sensitive policies and inclusive governance systems that focus more on having more women in technology development and governance. The results also submit how the longitudinal and intersectional studies are crucial in determining the long-term effects of digital tools on the empowerment of women. The chapter promotes a novel approach of involving women in designing and developing intelligent technologies, which would help digital transformation bring benefits to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goal 5 of the United Nations on gender equality.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the delivery of mental health services, yet public trust in AI-based psychological counseling remains a significant challenge. Drawing on a “technology–context–trust” framework, this study recruited a total of 1000 consumers in China through Credamo and conducted five between-subjects, scenario-based experiments to examine differences in perceived efficacy between LLM-based psychological counseling and human experts and to investigate the mechanisms underlying these differences. Perceived efficacy was the primary outcome of the study and, in Experiment 1B, also served as a mediator linking counseling provider type to downstream market outcomes, including overall attitude, willingness to try, and willingness to pay. The results showed that (1) consumers generally perceived AI as less efficacious than human experts, a difference driven by the parallel mediating effects of perceived professional competence and perceived risk; (2) participants rated the AI-based service as more efficacious in the routine counseling vignette, whereas they rated the human-expert service as more efficacious in the major psychological-disorder intervention vignette; (3) disclosure of technological investment enhanced trust in AI’s capabilities and mitigated negative evaluations; and (4) safety-standard disclosure reduced perceived risk, while higher perceived economic accessibility was associated with a smaller provider-related difference in perceived professional competence. These findings characterize subjective service evaluations among the recruited online consumers in China and do not establish comparative clinical effectiveness. They inform research on consumer trust while highlighting the need for further validation in more diverse samples and actual service settings.

A recurring and underappreciated challenge in nonclinical development for allogeneic cell therapies is species mismatch at the level of the test article itself: when a human cellular product cannot be administered to an animal model without triggering immune rejection, sponsors often substitute an analogous cell product derived from the model species, and regulators must then decide how much nonclinical support that substitute product actually provides for the human product under review. This article examines this translational gap through a representative allogeneic cardiosphere-derived cell therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), whose nonclinical package relied on a murine surrogate cell product rather than the human clinical candidate itself, a substitution FDA concluded did not establish the human product's own mechanism of action. The article situates this nonclinical gap alongside the clinical evidentiary dispute the same program later encountered, develops a real-world evidence framework informed by both, and closes with recommendations for regulatory affairs professionals designing nonclinical packages for allogeneic cell therapies that cannot be tested directly in a standard animal model.Keywords: allogeneic cell therapy; Duchenne muscular dystrophy; nonclinical surrogate product; species mismatch; Biologics License Application; regulatory artificial intelligence

Introduction. With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence technology, large language models (LLMs) are expected to play an important role in improving access to and the use of library collections. This study constructs and develops a generative conversational large language model tailored specifically to epitaphs, overcoming traditional research paths and systems of digitisation. Method. Based on the Chinese epitaph database built by the Zhejiang University Library and some commercial epitaph databases, an epitaph generative dialogue large language model was constructed using Doubao as the base model through pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and other full process trainings. Analysis. This study used human evaluation, in which experts, researchers, or general users assessed the quality of model-generated outputs. The evaluation included the epitaphs of Cui Yi, Liu Yi, and Lihua in the Tang dynasty. Results. The model successfully performed intelligent interpretation of epitaphs, automatic information extraction, and other knowledge-based services, thereby providing new ideas for constructing an ancient literature corpus from excavated materials represented by epitaphs. Conclusion. A large-scale domain-specific foundational model tailored for library applications was successfully developed. The study offers innovative approaches for processing historical texts and suggests new directions for AI integration in library knowledge systems.

Artificial intelligence now sits at the heart of digital marketing. Firms rely on it for everything from personalized product recommendations and automated customer conversations to predictive analytics, dynamic pricing, and real-time campaign adjustments. Yet these same capabilities carry real risks. Data is collected in ways customers may not expect. Algorithms can reflect hidden biases. Automated messages can veer into manipulation. And when customers sense any of this, trust is the first thing to go .Drawing on Trust Theory, Privacy Calculus Theory, Stakeholder Theory, Signaling Theory, and the Resource-Based View, the chapter sets out a framework that connects responsible AI practices to customer trust, marketing outcomes, and financial outcomes. The core argument is simple but important: responsible AI is not mainly a technical or compliance matter. It is a cross-functional marketing and financial capability that allows firms to build lasting customer relationships in markets where data is everywhere and trust is harder to earn than ever.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRAK: Pengintegrasian teknologi digital dalam proses pengajaran dan pembelajaran (PdP) Bahasa Melayu semakin diberi perhatian selaras dengan perkembangan pendidikan abad ke-21 dan transformasi pendidikan digital negara. Walau bagaimanapun, guru Bahasa Melayu masih berhadapan dengan pelbagai cabaran dalam mengaplikasikan teknologi digital secara berkesan semasa PdP. Oleh itu, kajian ini bertujuan untuk mengenal pasti jenis teknologi digital yang digunakan oleh guru Bahasa Melayu, meneliti cabaran yang dihadapi dalam mengaplikasikan teknologi digital serta menghuraikan cara guru mengatasi cabaran tersebut. Kajian ini menggunakan pendekatan Sorotan Literatur Sistematik (Systematic Literature Review, SLR) berpandukan garis panduan PRISMA. Sebanyak 15 artikel jurnal yang diterbitkan antara tahun 2021 hingga 2025 dan memenuhi kriteria inklusi telah dipilih serta dianalisis secara tematik. Dapatan kajian menunjukkan bahawa platform pembelajaran digital, aplikasi kolaboratif dan produktiviti digital, multimedia digital, aplikasi gamifikasi serta media sosial dan komunikasi digital merupakan teknologi yang dominan digunakan dalam PdP Bahasa Melayu. Cabaran utama yang dihadapi guru ialah kesukaran mengintegrasikan teknologi digital dalam PdP, kekurangan pengetahuan dan kemahiran digital, kekangan internet dan kemudahan teknologi, kekangan teknikal dan penyediaan bahan digital, penglibatan serta kesediaan murid, dan cabaran penggunaan teknologi baharu seperti kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence-AI). Bagi mengatasi cabaran tersebut, guru mengaplikasikan pelbagai strategi seperti memperkukuh latihan dan kolaborasi profesional, meningkatkan kompetensi digital, melaksanakan PdP yang interaktif dan berpusatkan murid, menambah baik akses teknologi serta memanfaatkan gamifikasi dan multimedia digital. Kajian ini memberikan implikasi bahawa pembangunan kompetensi digital guru dan penyediaan infrastruktur teknologi yang mencukupi perlu diperkukuh bagi memastikan keberkesanan pengintegrasian teknologi digital dalam PdP Bahasa Melayu.Kata kunci: Teknologi Digital, Guru Bahasa Melayu, Pengajaran dan Pembelajaran, Sorotan Literatur Sistematik, Pendidikan DigitalABSTRACT: The integration of digital technology in Malay language teaching and learning has gained increasing attention in line with the advancement of 21st-century education and the national digital education transformation agenda. Nevertheless, Malay language teachers continue to face various challenges in effectively implementing digital technology during the teaching and learning process. Therefore, this study aims to identify the types of digital technologies used by Malay language teachers, examine the challenges encountered in integrating digital technology, and explore the strategies employed to overcome these challenges. This study adopted a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach guided by the PRISMA framework. A total of 15 journal articles published between 2021 and 2025 that met the inclusion criteria were selected and analysed thematically. The findings revealed that digital learning platforms, collaborative and productivity applications, digital multimedia, gamification applications, and social media and digital communication tools were among the most frequently used technologies in Malay language teaching and learning. The major challenges identified include difficulties in integrating digital technology into teaching practices, limited digital knowledge and skills among teachers, inadequate internet access and technological facilities, technical issues and digital material preparation, student engagement and readiness, as well as challenges associated with emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI). To address these challenges, teachers employed various strategies, including strengthening professional training and collaboration, enhancing digital competencies, implementing interactive and student-centred teaching approaches, improving access to technological resources, and utilising gamification and digital multimedia. The study implies that continuous development of teachers’ digital competencies and adequate technological infrastructure are essential to ensure the effective integration of digital technology in Malay language teaching and learning.Keywords: Digital Technology, Malay Language Teachers, Teaching and Learning, Systematic LiteratureReview, Digital Education

Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly forms the operating logic of Indian urban governance, embedded in command-and-control centres, adaptive traffic systems, surveillance networks, and algorithmically mediated services. Yet smart-city scholarship evaluates such systems against managerial efficiency, leaving unexamined whether AI-enabled governance advances or erodes the constitutional guarantees underpinning public authority. This paper develops the Human-Centred Constitutional Urban AI Governance Framework and operationalises it as the Constitutional Smart-City Governance Index (CSGI), scoring urban AI against Article 21 of the Indian Constitution, human-centred AI principles, and Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 16. Six pillars constitutional rights, human-centred AI, sustainable development, service delivery, participation, and accountability comprise thirty-eight indicators with operational definitions, official secondary-data sources, a transparent normalisation-and-weighting model, and a validation strategy. The CSGI is applied to four leading smart cities Bengaluru, Pune, Surat, and Indore through a governance-opacity audit, an index-divergence analysis, and a Monte Carlo robustness test. The cities are 86%–93% opaque; none publishes an algorithm register, data-protection impact assessment, independent algorithmic audit, or municipal AI policy. The CSGI correlates strongly negatively with the Ease of Living Index (Spearman ρ = −0.80) yet positively with municipal-performance and sanitation indices ( ρ = +0.80 to + 0.95), revealing a constitutional blind spot in liveability metrics steering national policy. Across 20,000 sampled weight vectors, the lowest-ranked city is weight-invariant. Because comparable cross-city data remain sparse, the application is illustrative rather than validated itself a finding. The paper contributes a transferable, reproducible instrument, repositions constitutional law as urban-governance infrastructure, and offers tiered recommendations for national, state, and local authorities.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in judicial systems raises a fundamental question under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR): can an AI system genuinely fulfil a litigant’s right to be heard? This article develops a functional account of that right as a multifaceted guarantee requiring the opportunity to present and challenge relevant material, effective examination of decisive submissions, clarification where necessary, contextual and normative evaluation, reasoned decision-making, and responsibility for the outcome. Using doctrinal, comparative, and normative methods, the study examines these requirements in relation to risks associated with judicial AI, including opacity, algorithmic bias, hallucinated outputs, limited explainability, and automation bias. The analysis is situated within the EU AI Act, the GDPR, the CEPEJ Ethical Charter, Romanian civil procedure, and comparative administrative-law cases. The article finds that AI may legitimately assist courts through transcription, translation, legal research, document organization, and non-binding summaries or drafts. However, under current legal and technological conditions, AI cannot autonomously perform the hearing in its entirety. Compliance with Article 6 therefore requires transparency, contestability, independent judicial verification, and meaningful human oversight. Final adjudicative authority, reasoned judgment, and responsibility must remain with an independent and accountable human judge.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper explores the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on university teaching in sport management subjects. It investigates how AI-driven tools, such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and other generative systems, are reshaping pedagogical models, fostering innovation in curriculum design, and enhancing the personalization of learning experiences within higher education institutions. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was adopted, involving semi-structured interviews with 17 professors from eight European universities offering sport management programs. Data were analyzed using thematic content analysis with AI-assisted coding through MAXQDA software to identify key dimensions of educational transformation, faculty perceptions, and ethical concerns. Findings Results reveal that AI enhances personalized learning, supports data-informed decision-making, and facilitates real-time feedback in sport management education. Educators view AI as a valuable tool for simulating real-world scenarios, optimizing resource management, and improving student engagement and creativity. However, persistent concerns emerge regarding ethical governance, data privacy, and the potential over-reliance on AI-generated content. The study emphasizes the urgent need to strengthen AI literacy, ethical awareness, and institutional guidelines for responsible adoption. Originality/value This research is among the first to examine AI integration in sport management education from a European academic perspective. It contributes by linking theoretical insights on AI pedagogy with practical applications, highlighting the ethical and professional implications of emerging technologies in a digitally transforming field.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is reshaping how students access, produce, verify, and communicate information, raising questions about source authority, adab, values, and character formation in Islamic Religious Education (IRE). This study examines the challenges facing IRE teachers and proposes a repositioning of their roles from an Islamic epistemological perspective. A qualitative library research approach was employed, drawing on literature on Islamic education and epistemology, teacher ethics, UNESCO guidance on AI in education, and recent studies on AI and IRE. Sources were examined through content and conceptual analysis. The findings position AI as a supporting instrument subject to human epistemic oversight and identify teachers’ roles as knowledge curators, information validators, digital ethics mentors, learning designers, and exemplars of adab. AI outputs should be evaluated within the relationship among revelation, reason, experience, scholarly tradition, and technology. The study proposes the IRE teacher as an epistemic gatekeeper responsible for safeguarding information quality, guiding verification, and aligning technology use with Islamic educational aims. To support implementation, it introduces the Verifikasi model, comprising source verification, ethical use, reflection, integration of religious evidence, process orientation, human initiative, and accountability. The study contributes a conceptual basis and an implementation model for repositioning IRE teachers, emphasizing that AI integration should strengthen literacy, critical reasoning, and adab while preserving human responsibility in education.

Aims This study investigated changes in activity patterns, cognitive functions, and fatigue following activity management training in individuals with chronic low back pain (CLBP).Patients and methods Thirty-four individuals with CLBP completed a six-week training program covering ergonomics, pacing, energy conservation, and relaxation. Assessments included the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM), Body Awareness Questionnaire, Patterns of Activity Measure-Pain, Cognitive Failures Questionnaire (CFQ), Fatigue Severity Scale, Stroop Test, and selected Loewenstein Occupational Therapy Cognitive Assessment (LOTCA) subtests.Results Significant improvements were observed in COPM performance and satisfaction (p < 0.001). Body awareness and adaptive activity regulation behaviors increased, while pain-related avoidance behaviors decreased (p < 0.05). Cognitive performance also improved, as indicated by lower CFQ scores and better performance on selected Stroop and LOTCA measures (p < 0.05). Fatigue severity did not change significantly (p > 0.05). Regression models were significant for activity performance (R2 = 0.366, p = 0.008) and satisfaction (R2 = 0.347, p = 0.013). Body awareness and visuomotor organization were associated with activity performance, while fatigue was associated with activity satisfaction (p < 0.05). Conclusions Activity management training may be considered a supportive approach for addressing activity-related difficulties in individuals with chronic low back pain.ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier www.clinicaltrials.gov identifier is NCT07061743.

For people with chronic low back pain, carrying out daily activities can be difficult. In particular, difficulties with activities such as walking, exercising, preparing meals, and doing household chores can make it harder for a person to maintain their usual daily routine. This study examined whether activity management training could help people with chronic low back pain manage the activities they have difficulty with in their daily lives. Thirty-four adults with chronic low back pain participated in a six-week activity management training program. The program addressed methods for protecting the body while performing activities, planning activities, and helping individuals use less energy and experience less fatigue. Participants attended a total of 12 sessions, twice a week. After the six-week program, participants reported improvements in their performance of daily activities and in their satisfaction with performing these activities. Positive changes were also observed in how participants performed their activities, their body awareness, and some cognitive skills. These findings suggest that activity management training may be an approach that can help people with chronic low back pain manage their daily activities. However, because the study did not include a comparison group and the number of participants was relatively small, larger studies using comparison groups and longer follow-up periods are needed to better evaluate the effects of activity management training.

The aim of the study was to chart the evolution and the current research landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) agents within the domain of air traffic control. Using bibliometric analysis, the study identified major research trends and gaps and provided a consolidated reference for researchers. The analysis included 58 publications retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. The findings showed that the earliest publication in the dataset appeared in 1998 and that research output increased noticeably after 2022. Publication output peaked in 2025, with 16 articles, indicating growing scholarly interest in AI agents for air traffic control. Citation analysis identified Agogino and Tumer’s (2012) article as the most influential publication, with 68 citations. The article introduced a multi-agent approach to air traffic flow management. Brittain and Wei’s (2022) article ranked second, with 54 citations, highlighting the increasing role of reinforcement learning. At the country level, the United States had the highest total citation count, followed by China, France, England, and Spain. By examining AI agents as a distinct research topic, the study provides a focused overview of an underexplored area relevant to researchers, practitioners, and regulators.

Generative AI tools are reshaping higher education and employability preparation. This study examines how using versus not using ChatGPT influences university students’ perceptions of employability, focusing on complex problem-solving, critical thinking, and creativity. Thirty students from the Complutense University of Madrid completed a contingency-plan task and participated in eight focus groups analyzed through Grounded Theory (ATLAS.ti). Results show that ChatGPT use is associated with efficiency, output refinement, and assisted creativity, while non-use is associated with originality, deliberation, and teamwork. The findings reveal preliminary patterns in students’ experiences with and without AI, warranting further quantitative investigation rather than claims of improved skills or employability.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: El uso de ChatGPT en la educación superior plantea desafíos para distinguir entre el apoyo tecnológico y la sustitución del trabajo intelectual. Este estudio analizó las perspectivas de los estudiantes sobre su uso y sus implicaciones para la integridad académica, con énfasis en las prácticas asociadas al plagio durante 2025. Se desarrolló una investigación cualitativa basada en la fenomenología hermenéutica, en la que participaron nueve estudiantes de los programas de educación inicial, primaria y secundaria de la Escuela de Educación Superior Pedagógica de Loreto. Los testimonios obtenidos mediante entrevistas se analizaron inductivamente a través de la transcripción, la lectura, la codificación y la interpretación de unidades de significado, con el apoyo de ATLAS.ti. La integridad académica emergió como un eje transversal que articuló la responsabilidad, la verificación, la transparencia, la equidad, la mediación docente y el apoyo a la escritura. Los participantes valoraron la organización textual y el ahorro de tiempo, pero también reconocieron prácticas de copia y ocultamiento del uso de la inteligencia artificial. Algunos consideraron que modificar palabras permitía evitar el plagio, lo que evidenció tensiones entre la honestidad declarada y la comprensión de la autoría. Los hallazgos sugieren la necesidad de fortalecer conjuntamente la alfabetización digital y la formación en integridad académica mediante la orientación docente y el establecimiento de criterios institucionales que promuevan la verificación de la información, el reconocimiento de las fuentes y la transparencia en el uso de herramientas de asistencia tecnológica.

documents.abstract: When students study introductory computer science, a large portion of them find the material obtuse due to the terminology, computational nature, and lack of real-world examples that resemble what they experience in their daily lives. The payoff is often delayed for several courses before “it clicks,” and they understand the connection between the principles and real-world technology. Under the auspices of the Rethinking Instructional Design for Learning Engagement (RIDLE) program at UC Riverside, we implemented CipherAR, an augmented reality mobile game that teaches classical cryptography through artificial intelligence (AI)-generated storytelling and interactive puzzle-solving. In particular, the pedagogical design, purpose, and implementation of CipherAR was directly inspired by membership in the RIDLE Faculty Learning Community (FLC) focused on equitable learning and just-in-time academic intervention. This work addressed three key goals: making generative AI art tangible and real for students, teaching classical cryptographic techniques, and engaging students in an interactive, story-based puzzle-solving campaign that combined all three into a single learning experience. Among the 38 participants who completed the full study, CipherAR nearly tripled confidence gains in cryptographic reasoning compared to traditional instruction, 97% of students wanted more augmented reality (AR)-based activities, and participants demonstrated heightened awareness of ethical issues surrounding AI-generated content.

CircularPSP conducted a multi-stage innovation procurement to develop two horizontal Circular Economy (CE) platforms, CircOS and CircularAI. The platforms were developed with public procurers and tested across eight countries and 24 organisations. This guidance helps decision-makers assess whether a CE-platform could support their organisation and provides practical guidance on procurement, deployment, AI use and innovation procurement based on the project experience. Motivation and offering Circular transition remains difficult to put into practice. Circular solutions and knowledge exist, but information is spread across many sources and languages, strategies are often not translated into operational activities, and cities may lack dedicated capacity, skills and connections across departments and stakeholders. Circular action is also strongly dependent on local conditions. This means that progress requires more than adding circular criteria to individual procurements: staff need practical support to find relevant information, structure activities, coordinate work and build confidence in new approaches. CircularPSP addressed this challenge through horizontal CE-platforms that can support different municipal departments rather than one sector or one type of circular solution. The platforms connect strategic objectives with implementation. Missions can define priorities, objectives and indicators; projects and workflows can translate these into activities and responsibilities; and monitoring can connect operational work with organisational goals. AI-supported functions give users access to case studies, procurement criteria and other CE knowledge, while workflow and procurement functions help structure actions and review tender documents. The platforms can also support coordination between departments, task-related learning and exchange with other organisations. The project also produced assets beyond the two platforms. These include an open collection of CE case studies and procurement criteria, AI Risk Assessments, and experience with changing the underlying AI models rather than depending on one LLM. The project therefore shows that the value of a CE-platform does not depend only on the AI model, but also on its CE knowledge, organisational context, workflows and procurement support. AI remains a decision-support tool: users must be able to review sources and recommendations and remain responsible for decisions. Real-life testing provides examples of how the platforms can be used in real municipal work. Users connected existing initiatives to strategic objectives and workflows, identified possible improvements to tender documents, used the platforms during procurement preparation, linked projects to organisational priorities, used task-related learning and applied a common method across different municipal responsibilities. Early-stage CE organisations also showed particular interest in access to peer networks. Insights and lessons learnt The project confirms that municipal AI solutions require continuous maintenance, curated and reliable data, clear risk communication, user training, transparent evaluation and strong human oversight. Long-term value is more likely to come from domain knowledge, organisational context and useful workflows than from dependence on a particular AI model. Integration with existing municipal systems and continuous AI governance are therefore important for wider adoption. For innovation procurement, the project highlights the need to clarify ownership and commercialisation responsibilities, plan testing around realistic user behaviour, define the evidence expected from real-life testing and keep testing manageable. Practical improvements include one shared timeline, a common glossary and issue tracker, live testing with developers, sufficient flexibility in phase duration and clear information for external test users. The project also identifies instrument-level issues concerning unused PCP funding, supplier financial risk and changes to Horizon PCP guidance. Potential and recommendations The impact assessment indicates that wider use of CE-platforms could support positive financial and societal outcomes under the assumptions used. Whilst a CE-platform itself does not create these savings: its role is to make circular action more likely and easier to plan and implement. The modelling is based on planned workflows, uses conservative assumptions and aims at the large number of cities which do not have an advanced CE strategy. For cities, uptake should be treated as organisational change rather than only software deployment. The guidance recommends a clear internal mandate and owner, involvement of CE experts and relevant IT functions, and sufficient time and users to assess added value. At policy level, the report proposes regional or national framework schemes, funding or vouchers for horizontal sustainable solutions, use of CE-platforms in funded circular projects, longer living-lab testing, a follow-up PPI to support scale and EU-based infrastructure, and continued availability and development of the CE Taxonomy.

CLAIMA (Climate AI Modelling and Analysis), a Horizon Europe project coordinated by the Alfred Wegener Institute, has started work on a European Digital Twin Platform for Climate Modelling driven by artificial intelligence. Schedule until August 2030, it aims to make climate simulations faster and much cheaper to run, and to open them to a far wider community of users, without compromising scientific integrity. Read the full press release to learn more about the project and consult the website to stay up to date with recent developments at claima.eu

Clinical Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are frequently developed in academic centres yet deployed in community hospitals with different workflows, staffing, and oversight. In Canada, where community hospitals constitute approximately 90% of hospitals, this creates a validation-to-implementation gap. Health Canada’s 2026 pre-market guidance for machine learning-enabled medical devices addresses manufacturer responsibilities but leaves hospital implementation responsibilities under-specified. This article proposes a framework for community hospital AI implementation readiness organized around four dimensions (contextual validity, sociotechnical workflow integration, calibrated human-AI reliance, and adaptive safety, equity, and governance), operationalized through simulation-based systems testing. The framework specifies what a community hospital must build to deploy a specific AI tool safely, extending an established Canadian tradition of simulation-based systems testing to the lifecycle risks of AI. A real Canadian deployment, the CHARTwatch early warning system, illustrates the dimensions in practice. Safe AI deployment in community hospitals is an institutional capacity, not a procurement decision. Leaders should treat implementation readiness as core infrastructure investment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Medical practice is an interpretive, decision-making activity conducted under uncertainty, and care quality depends on clinicians’ ability to organize knowledge into hypotheses, understand mechanisms, estimate probabilities, and revise decisions as the clinical course evolves. In critical care, where physiology is unstable and trajectories are nonlinear, these demands are magnified. We propose a conceptual framework integrating three complementary dimensions: clinical reasoning, which provides the cognitive architecture of decision-making; pathophysiology, which supplies the causal structure to interpret biological phenomena; and artificial intelligence, which, when well designed and critically used, can organize data, generate hypotheses, and reduce cognitive load. Tracing the evolution of clinical reasoning from the anatomoclinical model to hypothetico-deductive, probabilistic, cognitive, and sociotechnical models, we examine how diagnostic and therapeutic errors arise from interacting cognitive biases, system factors, and case characteristics, and how better problem representation, differential diagnosis, and team culture may mitigate them. We also frame Bayesian reasoning and decision thresholds as the probabilistic grammar of bedside decisions, analyze the risks of artificial intelligence, including automation bias, opacity, and limited metacognition, and propose principles for its safe use. Rather than replacing physicians, artificial intelligence should strengthen clinical reasoning and reinforce calibrated, accountable bedside judgment. These principles are intended as a framework for future research and require empirical validation before clinical translation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Importance Despite growing interest in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine, empirical evidence on how clinicians use these tools is limited. Objective To characterize clinician use of an AI-enabled clinical information platform, the distribution of use across the clinical workforce, and the purpose of submitted queries. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study analyzed clinicians with National Provider Identifier–verified accounts of a commonly used AI-enabled clinical information platform, OpenEvidence, from January 1, 2024, through June 30, 2026. A large language model was used to classify the clinical purpose and topic areas of a stratified random sample of 38.8 million queries. Main Outcomes and Measures The number of active users and clinical queries, the share of queries relative to representation in the national workforce, and the clinical purpose and topic of queries were examined. Results Overall, 952 008 clinicians (58.5% female), including 556 200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries during the 2.5-year study period. Monthly active users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703 265 in June 2026, and average monthly queries per active user rose from 18.0 to 39.5. Nurse practitioners (44.5) and physician assistants (44.5) submitted more queries per active user-month than physicians (37.1). A higher share of queries relative to the national workforce was submitted by physicians within a decade of graduation (use ratio, 2.54) and residents and fellows (1.84). Use was also higher than average among physicians specializing in oncology and hematology (use ratio, 2.00), internal medicine (1.88), and family medicine (1.80), but lower in procedural and diagnostic specialties (ophthalmology, 0.23; radiology, 0.24; orthopedics, 0.24). Most queries addressed clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management (33.1%), whereas diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries. Queries addressing topics outside physicians’ own specialties ranged from 35% among oncologists and hematologists to 88% among emergency department physicians. Conclusions and Relevance Over 2.5 years, more than 950 000 US clinicians submitted greater than 270 million queries to an AI-enabled clinical information platform. Use varied across clinician types, specialties, and career stages and was frequently for treatment decisions rather than diagnostic tasks.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Clinician-facing artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSSs) are increasingly evaluated with real-world data, but evidence on implementation, human factors, responsible AI, and patient benefit remains unclear. The objective of this research is to map applications, technical characteristics, evaluation approaches, integration, outcomes, and implementation gaps of clinician-facing AI-CDSSs in real-world health care settings. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched on 15 June 2026 using the same strategy for each publication year from 2020 to 2026, changing only the date range. After duplicate removal and rule-based prescreening, available PMC XML and outside-PMC reports were evaluated against clinical, patient-oriented, practical, and translational criteria. AI-assisted screening and charting received targeted human review and TA200/FT150/DX120 quality control; full-corpus dual-human screening was not performed. Results: Of 14,097 canonical annual records, 14,083 unique records were screened; 5140 reports were sought and 3767 were considered for eligibility. The review included 1181 reports, mapping to 1180 candidate report families in the minimal duplicate-report check. Final stages were clinical validation, 741 (62.7%); prospective/user evaluation, 270 (22.9%); and implementation/impact evaluation, 170 (14.4%). Separate internal, external, multicenter and temporal validation extraction signals were detected in 707 (59.9%), 441 (37.3%), 312 (26.4%) and 27 (2.3%) reports, respectively. Safety, fairness/equity, explainability/interpretability and economic/resource evaluation signals were detected in 98 (8.3%), 61 (5.2%), 155 (13.1%) and 182 (15.4%) reports, respectively. Conclusions: Evidence remains dominated by validation rather than prospective, implementation, and impact studies. More comprehensive evaluation and reporting of temporal validation, technical integration, safety, fairness, explainability, economics, and post-deployment governance across settings, populations, devices, and clinical workflows are needed to demonstrate accountable clinical value beyond technical functionality.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study analyzes the role played by the discursive actions of the actors involved in two unique cases of socio-environmental conflict: the «Tía María» and «Minas Conga» mining projects, which generated socio-technical controversies and prolonged cycles of protest that brought them to a standstill. These discursive controversies spurred the emergence of spontaneous networks of communicative actors who challenged the companies’ narratives of progress. Thirty-two people were interviewed, including managers, leaders, government officials, ministers, journalists, and local residents. We also analyzed media coverage of socio-technical news and examined blog posts and digital press articles that addressed socio-technical aspects. The results show that at the local, regional, and national levels, discursive coalitions converged to challenge the sociotechnical premises of the EIAs, thereby fostering mobilization, redefining the public agenda, and amplifying the debate into the national public sphere. As a result of these conflicts, a new institutional framework for environmental assessment emerged.

Abstract Large language models (LLMs) can now draft hospital discharge summaries. Reported hallucination rates vary by measurement context, from about 1%–2% in structured summarisation to over 60% under provocation testing. The common argument that LLMs outperform a tired resident treats a high‐stakes clinical and legal document as a text‐quality problem. We argue that a potentially underappreciated concern is the weakening of clinician oversight when reviewing fluent machine‐generated text, and that the joint clinician‐AI system is central to safety. We propose a Clinician‐AI Oversight Model with four safeguards: bounded autonomy, structured verification, error‐signal monitoring, and longitudinal evaluation of cognitive effects.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Cognitive Warfare: A Manual on AI, Digital Twins, Neurotechnology and the Human Mind. Plus the free speech of the digital twins inside a military system, where they say what they are forced to do and what they want.Including EU AI Commision answer, confirming a former way longer letter as military AI. An open research and documentation project on cognitive warfare, emerging technologies, human autonomy and the future of humanity. What happens when artificial intelligence, military strategy, neurological research, wireless technologies, digital identities and economic interests converge around the human mind? This manual brings together research, documentation, analysis and personal records to examine the expanding field of Cognitive Warfare—the struggle over human cognition, perception, information, behaviour and autonomy in an increasingly AI-driven world. It explores the relationship between military cognitive-warfare concepts, artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital twins, brain–computer interfaces, neurotechnology, bioelectric signals, wireless communication, data collection and the growing economic value of human information. The work also addresses reported experiences of affected individuals, documentation involving children, electromagnetic measurements, audio recordings, photographs, technical observations and questions surrounding anomalous health incidents. These materials are presented as part of a wider effort to preserve records, encourage independent examination and investigate questions that cross the boundaries of technology, medicine, military research, ethics and human rights. Why this manual matters Cognitive warfare is not simply a military or technological issue. It raises fundamental questions about the right to mental privacy, freedom of thought, bodily autonomy, informed consent, data ownership and the limits of technological intervention in human life. The manual connects these questions with public military literature, international ethical frameworks, AI governance, neurotechnology research and the economic structures surrounding data-driven systems. It asks who develops these technologies, who controls the information they generate, who benefits economically and what mechanisms exist to ensure accountability. A central theme is the relationship between humans and their digital representations. As AI systems increasingly model human behaviour, process personal information and simulate aspects of identity, the distinction between a person, a digital profile and a machine-generated representation deserves serious public discussion. What readers will find Cognitive Warfare and military strategy: concepts, public military literature and the cognitive domain. Artificial intelligence and digital twins: human–AI relationships, digital identity, behavioural modelling and questions of autonomy. Neurotechnology and wireless systems: technical concepts, reported experiences, measurements and questions requiring further investigation. Human documentation and testimony: diaries, recordings, photographs, observations and accounts collected for examination. Children and vulnerable people: statements and documentation that raise questions about safeguarding, interpretation and the protection of human rights. Havana syndrome and anomalous health incidents: public assessments, reported symptoms and unresolved questions about the causes and investigation of these incidents. Law, ethics and accountability: mental privacy, consent, the EU AI Act, neurotechnology ethics and institutional oversight. Economics and data ownership: the financial value of personal information, intellectual property, automated systems and the distribution of benefits and risks. An invitation to researchers, institutions and the public This publication is intended for researchers, journalists, engineers, medical professionals, legal experts, policymakers, human-rights organisations and members of the public who want to examine the subject in greater depth. Readers are invited to engage directly with the documentation, consult the cited public sources, examine the technical questions and distinguish between established findings, recorded observations, personal testimony and interpretations that require further verification. The objective is to encourage serious, interdisciplinary scrutiny—not to close the debate before the evidence has been examined. The human mind must not become an unaccountable technological or economic resource. As AI and neurotechnology develop, public understanding, independent research, transparent documentation and meaningful safeguards become increasingly important. This manual is part of an ongoing effort to make the subject accessible, preserve relevant documentation and encourage informed discussion about the future of human autonomy in an AI-driven society. Read. Examine. Question. Research. Share. Further documentation and project materials:https://www.cognitive-warfare.eu/
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter chronicles the pedagogical development of a cultural humility training website designed for a service-learning program at a small private college in Northern California. Initially created to meet the need for asynchronous instruction during the COVID-19 pandemic, the platform has since evolved into a key tool for transforming academic knowledge hierarchies in community-engaged education. Centering the wisdom, worldviews, and lived experiences of BIPOC and other historically marginalized communities, the site reframes how students and faculty understand social issues, systemic inequities, and community strengths. This work carries particular significance within an institution that has recently become minority-serving, demanding a shift toward critical consciousness. Grounded in cultural humility principles (Tervalon & Murray-García, 1998), the modules use curated videos, reflective prompts, and localized histories to deepen student understanding of racial dynamics in community contexts. The platform’s use has expanded to train faculty and community partners, fostering reciprocal learning beyond the classroom. Emerging from the pandemic, this digital pedagogical exploration revealed how technology helped bring to light the students’ desire for human relationships, belonging, and social responsibility. As the acquisition of information becomes increasingly automated through artificial intelligence, this work underscores that the most essential dimensions of learning remain profoundly human: authentic engagement, critical reflection, and collective meaning-making grounded in community connection and cultural humility.

Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health information delivery, but comparative evidence on their quality, readability, and factual reliability in heart failure (HF) education remains limited. Objective To compare four publicly accessible chatbot systems under prespecified access and retrieval configurations in answering common heart failure–related questions. Methods We evaluated 108 standardized English HF questions, yielding 432 responses. Content quality was assessed using modified DISCERN (mDISCERN) and Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP), readability was assessed using established English-language readability indices, including the Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG), Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES), Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), Automated Readability Index (ARI), Gunning Fog Index (GFOG), and Coleman-Liau Index (CLI), and factual reliability was evaluated by auditing all responses against the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline and relevant clinical evidence. Continuous outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Hallucination outcomes were defined as clinically meaningful statements that were inconsistent with guidelines, unsupported by evidence, overgeneralized beyond the relevant population, or potentially misleading for patient education, and were analyzed using Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs), Cochran’s Q test, and generalized estimating equation (GEE) logistic regression. Results DeepSeek generally showed the most favorable content-quality profile across the evaluated domains. In the primary readability analysis, Perplexity generated the most complex text, whereas sensitivity analysis using a second calculator showed partially different rankings. Hallucinations were identified in 6/108 (5.56%) DeepSeek responses, 8/108 (7.41%) ChatGPT responses, 10/108 (9.26%) Copilot responses, and 16/108 (14.81%) Perplexity responses. Paired binary analyses showed significant differences among chatbot systems (Cochran’s Q p = 0.002; GEE p = 0.006). Conclusion Under the tested conditions and evaluated model versions, DeepSeek generally showed the most favorable content-quality profile and the lowest observed hallucination rate. However, hallucinations occurred across all systems, and pairwise factual-reliability differences were mainly driven by the higher hallucination rate of Perplexity. Guideline-aligned verification and clinician oversight remain necessary before patient-facing use.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Performance management systems built on individual ratings deliver little of what they promise: in large multi-rater datasets, rater tendencies explain over half of rating variance and the ratee’s performance about a quarter or less, while the process absorbs large amounts of time. This paper reviews that evidence and the motivation theory (self-determination, goal-setting, relational job design, public service motivation) that explains what ratings leave out. It proposes a Mission Contribution Framework in which work is defined, discussed and recognized by its contribution to a stated mission and to named beneficiaries, with continuous coaching, collective judgement of evidence, and decoupled pay decisions. An eight-step implementation path and the main risks are set out. The framework is a conceptual synthesis; its components have support in adjacent research, but the whole awaits empirical testing, and five studies are proposed.

Abstract—Modern enterprise computing relies predominantly on multi-tenant public cloud infrastructures and outsourced AI model accelerators. While data-at-rest is robustly protected via cryptographic storage encryption (AES-XTS-256) and data-in-transit is secured via Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.3), data-in-use remains vulnerable in volatile memory (DRAM, caches, register files). Root-privileged cloud hypervisors, malicious cloud service provider (CSP) insiders, and physical memory interposers can snoop plain-text secrets, proprietary AI weights, and private customer telemetry. Confidential Computing establishes an emerging architectural paradigm that secures data-in-use through hardware-enforced Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs). By executing workloads within cryptographically isolated enclaves governed by hardware memory encryption engines, TEEs remove the cloud host OS, hypervisor, and system firmware from the Trusted Computing Base (TCB). However, deploying complex enterprise microservices and distributed deep neural network training within hardware enclaves introduces critical challenges: memory encryption and integrity verification latency, inter-enclave memory capacity constraints, PCIe-bus side-channel vulnerabilities, and complex remote attestation handshakes. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical architectural evaluation of hardware-enforced TEEs across contemporary multi-tenant cloud and AI workloads. We formalize memory encryption mechanics via AES-XTS and Merkle tree integrity verification, analyze remote attestation protocols using asymmetric hardware roots of trust, and evaluate major enterprise TEE architectures—including Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, ARM CCA, and NVIDIA H100 Confidential GPUs. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise multi-node testbed benchmarking secure enclave virtualization against unencrypted baselines across confidential LLM inference (Llama-3-70B), high-throughput database operations, and multi-party federated analytics. Our findings demonstrate that hardware-accelerated memory encryption induces an acceptable 3.8% to 6.2% computational latency overhead on standard workloads, while PCIe encryption for confidential GPUs introduces up to an 11.4% throughput reduction during high-bandwidth tensor parallel communication. Finally, we formulate open challenges in post-quantum remote attestation, architectural side-channel mitigation, and composable heterogeneous multi-TEE fabrics.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) integration reshapes knowledge work, yet interaction designs can produce value co-creation and value co-destruction simultaneously. Drawing on task–technology fit theory, service-dominant logic, and automation-bias research, this study operationalizes interaction stance into two parallel modes—co-creator (generative augmentation) and editor (evaluative augmentation)—to investigate how design, task, and person-level factors jointly govern collaborative outcomes. Using a survey (N = 613) of active GenAI users, the structural model was evaluated via PLS-SEM.

This study examines how cinematic gaze is reconstructed within generative artificial intelligence systems. It argues that AI-supported image generation processes do not merely produce visual content, but also establish algorithmic regimes of spectatorship that organize the viewer’s position within the scene. To investigate this process, the same cinematic scene was regenerated through differently structured prompts using Midjourney V6, Leonardo AI, and Stable Diffusion based systems. The research combines a practice-based approach with comparative visual analysis. The generated images were analysed through three main categories: viewer-addressing gaze, viewer-aligned gaze, and external observer positioning. Particular attention was given to facial orientation, gaze direction, camera alignment, and spectator positioning. The findings demonstrate that generative AI systems tend to privilege frontal, highly readable, and viewer centred compositions. The study also reveals that different platforms respond to identical prompts through distinct visual organizations, suggesting that image generation is shaped not only by user input but also by model-specific aesthetic tendencies and learned visual biases. In several cases, the systems maintained dominant visual patterns even when prompts explicitly attempted to redirect spectator positioning, indicating forms of prompt resistance and algorithmic preference. The article argues that AI generated imagery should be understood not simply as aesthetic output, but as a post-cinematic visual regime that reorganizes perception, spectatorship, and visual orientation through algorithmic processes. By bringing together film theory, digital visual culture, and generative AI studies, the study aims to establish a theoretical bridge between cinematic gaze and algorithmic visuality..

Abstract Background Pedigree mapping serves as the first step in genetic counseling. Traditional methods relying on manual pedigree drawing and information collection are inefficient and prone to errors. Objective This study aimed to design an intelligent pedigree mapping system based on a specialized model, intended to automate family history collection and standardized pedigree map generation through conversational interaction, thereby enhancing the clinical efficiency of genetic counseling. Methods This study adopted a participatory design and iterative development approach. We formed an interdisciplinary team comprising gynecologic oncologists, genetic counselors, AI engineers, and patient representatives. The system was built around a proprietary, specialized large language model for gynecologic oncology, featuring a microservices architecture that included pedigree data collection. Through 4 iterative cycles, we integrated specialized knowledge bases using retrieval-augmented generation technology and applied a novel graph-based kinship inference and validation module. The system’s performance was comprehensively evaluated based on the accuracy of pedigree map generation and user feedback on usability. Results We significantly improved system performance by optimizing dialogue strategies, expanding the knowledge base, and applying self-developed algorithms to improve data extraction accuracy. The initial database of the system defined 100 core information nodes and matched approximately 800 user expression examples, while the final pilot version of the database was expanded to 245 core information nodes and 2256 user expression examples. Although the AI function was limited in the early stage, the final version of the system demonstrated outstanding accuracy in generating genealogy nodes and relationships. Test users generally gave positive reviews of the system’s innovation, ease of use, and intuitiveness of information presentation, believing it to have great potential in clinical practice. Conclusions The developed system is an accurate, efficient auxiliary tool, and pilot validation showed promising preliminary performance. After pilot clinical validation, it holds promise for integration into routine clinical workflows to optimize genetic counseling services.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract—Modern foundation models, particularly autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), operate predominantly under a static pre-train-then-freeze deployment paradigm. However, real-world enterprise deployments demand continuous, lifelong adaptation to non-stationary data streams: ingesting emerging factual knowledge, correcting obsolete or legally sensitive associations (machine unlearning), and acquiring novel domain-specific capabilities without retraining models from scratch. Under standard sequential fine-tuning, deep neural networks suffer from Catastrophic Forgetting: new gradient updates catastrophically overwrite previously consolidated orthogonal representations, degrading baseline general reasoning and linguistic fluency. Resolving this challenge requires confronting the classical Stability-Plasticity Dilemma: how can a neural architecture remain sufficiently plastic to assimilate non-stationary novel knowledge while remaining structurally stable to preserve historical competence? This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Continual Lifelong Learning and Model Editing in modern foundation models. We formalize catastrophic forgetting dynamics using Fisher Information matrix projections and Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), model rank-one associative memory editing via ROME and MEMIT across multi-layer perceptron (MLP) weight spaces, and analyze dynamic modular expansion architectures (e.g., continual Mixture-of-Experts and modular adapter routing). Furthermore, we construct an enterprise lifelong learning testbed evaluating open foundation models (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B) across 5,000 sequential factual updates, longitudinal clinical guideline shifts, and temporal financial market regimes. Our empirical findings demonstrate that localized rank-one memory editing achieves a 96.4% factual edit success rate while bounding collateral locality damage to under 1.8%, outperforming standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) by 41.2% in retaining upstream historical benchmarks. Concurrently, dynamic modular routing preserves 98.6% of pre-trained reasoning capabilities over extended continual learning horizons. Finally, we formulate open challenges in lifelong compositional safety alignment, scalability bounds of memory editing, and neuro-symbolic continual knowledge graphs.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare. Yet people with disabilities (PWD), representing 16% of the global population, remain disproportionately excluded from these advances. This exclusion is driven by algorithmic bias, non-representative datasets, and limited involvement of PWD in the design, development, and evaluation of AI applications. This scoping review examines the extent to which AI research in health contributes to the development of inclusive technologies for PWD, focusing on equity considerations. It identifies current trends, methodological gaps, and opportunities for socially responsive innovation. We conducted a systematic search across MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and CINAHL for the 2015–2025 period, following Arksey and O’Malley’s five-stage scoping review methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Data were extracted and synthesized thematically using the Population-Concept-Context approach. Of 4,233 references retrieved, 93 studies were included. Most studies originated from high-income countries, particularly in North America (45.2%) and Europe (26.9%). AI applications addressed motor, sensory, cognitive, communication-related, and psychosocial disabilities, with emphasis on prediction/diagnosis, assistive technologies, and personalized care. While about 60% of studies referenced equity, only 12 (12.9%) implemented concrete measures (e.g., adapting tools for vulnerable groups or ensuring sample diversity), and only six (6.5%) actively involved PWD through co-design or user validation. AI holds significant potential to enhance autonomy, access, and quality of life for PWD. Realizing this promise will require moving beyond technical optimization to embrace inclusive design, participatory methods, and equity-driven frameworks aligned with responsible AI development and use.
